Stainless steel crowns can be used as a semi-permanent measure in children [2]. Microabrasion may help if discolouration is limited to the outer enamel layer [3].
problems.prognosis: The insult is past and no further hypoplasia develops. The clinical challenge is preventing secondary caries in the porous or deficient enamel and managing sensitivity.

citations.quote: So called because the hypoplastic enamel occurs in a distribution related to the extent of tooth formation at the time of the insult. Characteristically, due to its later formation, 2 is affected nearer to the incisal edge than 1 or 3.

Small areas of hypoplasia can be fissure-sealed or restored conventionally, but more severely affected teeth may require crowning. Stainless steel (SS) crowns can be used in children as a semi-permanent measure.

This is indicated for fluorosis, post-orthodontic demineralization, localized hypoplasia due to infection or trauma, and idiopathic hypoplasia where discoloration is limited to the outer enamel layer.

problems.description: Pitted, grooved, or thinned enamel on one or more teeth — the normal smooth enamel surface is structurally disrupted.
problems.etiology: Caused by a disturbance in enamel matrix formation [1]. The result is enamel that is structurally deficient in volume rather than just mineral content — pitted, grooved, or thinned. Most disturbances of enamel formation produce both hypoplasia and hypomineralisation, but clinically one type usually predominates [2]. Hypocalcification produces enamel that is white, yellow, or brown and opaque, may become more discoloured post-eruptively, and is weak and prone to breakdown [2].
problems.presentation: Pitting, grooving, or thinning of the enamel surface, visible on inspection. The teeth may be sensitive. Associated discolouration depends on whether hypomineralisation is also present: affected enamel appears white, yellow, or brown and opaque [2]. Breakdown can occur post-eruptively as structurally weakened enamel cannot withstand occlusal or erosive forces.
problems.results: Clinical examination identifies the enamel defect. Vitality is normal unless secondary caries has developed. Radiograph shows the extent of any structural deficiency and rules out pulpal involvement.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Hypoplasia is characterised by a quantity deficiency (thinned or absent enamel), whereas hypomineralisation is a quality deficiency (normal thickness, reduced mineral) [1][2]. In practice the two co-exist, but the predominant clinical appearance separates them.
problems.treatment: Treatment depends on extent and severity [3]. Small areas: fissure seal or conventional restoration. Severely affected posterior teeth may need crowning; stainless steel crowns serve as a semi-permanent solution in children [3]. Microabrasion for outer-layer discolouration limited to the enamel surface [4].
problems.prognosis: Stable once eruption is complete — no new hypoplasia develops. The main risks are secondary caries in pitted enamel and progressive breakdown if the structural deficiency is severe.

citations.quote: Caused by disturbance in matrix formation and is characterized by pitted, grooved, or thinned enamel.

Hypocalcification is a disturbance of calcification. Affected enamel appears white, yellow, or brown and opaque. May become more discoloured post-eruptively. Affected enamel may be weak and prone to breakdown. Most disturbances of enamel formation will produce both hypoplasia and hypomineralization, but clinically one type usually predominates.

Small areas of hypoplasia can be fissure-sealed or restored conventionally, but more severely affected teeth may require crowning. Stainless steel (SS) crowns can be used in children as a semi-permanent measure.

This is indicated for fluorosis, post-orthodontic demineralization, localized hypoplasia due to infection or trauma, and idiopathic hypoplasia where discoloration is limited to the outer enamel layer.

problems.description: Abnormal-looking enamel on many or all teeth — may be thin, pitted, rough, opaque white, honey-coloured, or prone to rapid chipping — affecting both primary and permanent dentitions.
problems.etiology: A group of inherited disorders of enamel formation. Mutations in at least 15 different genes are associated with amelogenesis imperfecta, with commonly affected genes including AMELX, ENAM, AMBN, KLK4, and MMP20 [1]. Main subtypes: hypoplastic (enamel may be thin, smooth or rough, or pitted; most commonly autosomal dominant [2]); hypocalcified (enamel dull, lustreless, opaque white, honey, or brown coloured; may break down rapidly in severe cases; sensitivity and calculus increased [3]); and hypomaturation (mottled or frosty-looking white opacities, sometimes confined to the incisal third — 'snow-capped teeth' [4]).
problems.presentation: Both primary and secondary dentitions are affected, and all teeth are usually involved [5]. The clinical picture varies widely across subtypes — from mild discolouration to severely deficient enamel broken down across most of the dentition [5]. Sensitivity is common, particularly in the hypocalcified type [3].
problems.results: Clinical examination reveals the full extent of enamel involvement across all teeth. Radiographs may show reduced enamel density or contrast in hypomineralised subtypes. Enamel-renal syndrome (FAM20A gene mutation) is a rare subtype with associated nephrocalcinosis: clinical features include intra-pulpal calcification, hyperplastic dental follicles, delayed eruption, and gingival hyperplasia — suspected cases need genetic confirmation and renal investigation [6].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The distinction from MIH is that amelogenesis imperfecta affects all teeth in both dentitions, not just first molars and incisors [5]. Fluorosis produces symmetrical white mottling but not the breakdown or near-absent enamel of severe hypocalcified or hypoplastic subtypes. Enamel-renal syndrome is the rare hypoplastic subtype warranting renal referral alongside dental management [6].
problems.treatment: Seek specialist advice for all but the mildest forms [5]. In more severe cases, stainless steel crowns and composite resin can be used to maintain molars and permanent incisors prior to more permanent restorations when the child is older [5]. Early recognition is important to prevent rapid tooth wear [7].
problems.prognosis: Without early protective restorations, rapid and severe tooth wear leads to loss of vertical dimension and extensive dentine exposure [7]. With appropriate restorative management, the dentition can be preserved, though lifelong restorative needs are the norm for moderate to severe cases.

citations.quote: Many classifications exist, but generally these are classified by the type of enamel defect &/or the mode of inheritance. There are now known to be mutations in at least 15 different genes that are associated with AI8 (commonly affected genes: AMELX, ENAM, AMBN, KLK4, MMP20).
Hypoplastic—enamel may be thin (smooth or rough) or pitted. Most commonly autosomal dominant inheritance.

Hypocalcified—enamel is dull, lustreless, opaque white, honey, or brown coloured. Enamel may breakdown rapidly in severe cases. Sensitivity i, calculus ↑ common. May be autosomal dominant or recessive.
Hypomaturation—mottled or frosty-looking white opacities, sometimes confined to incisal third of crown ('snow-capped teeth').

Usually both 1° and 2° dentitions and all the teeth are affected. The different subgroups give rise to a wide variation in clinical presentation, ranging from discoloration to soft &/or deficient enamel. It is therefore difficult to make general recommendations, but it is wise to seek specialist advice for all but the mildest forms. Rx: in more severe cases, SS crowns and composite resin can be used to maintain molars and 2° inc, prior to more permanent restorations when child is older.

Enamel-renal syndrome: a rare hypoplastic AI caused by mutation of the FAM20A gene and associated with nephrocalcinosis. Suspected individuals should be referred for genetic confirmation, and if confirmed, renal investigation. Clinical features may include severely hypoplasic and discoloured enamel, semi-lunar shape of incisal edges, intra-pulpal calcification, hyperplastic dental follicles, delayed eruption, and gingival hyperplasia.
Early recognition and Rx of amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta is important to prevent rapid tooth wear.

problems.description: All the teeth have an unusual blue-brown or opalescent hue, the enamel chips off easily, and the underlying dentine wears rapidly — affecting the whole dentition in both generations of the family.
problems.etiology: More common than amelogenesis imperfecta, affecting approximately 1 in 8,000 [1]. Both primary and permanent dentitions are involved, although later-formed teeth may be less severely so [1]. Type I is associated with osteogenesis imperfecta [2]; Type II affects teeth only [3]. Osteogenesis imperfecta involves an autosomal dominant type 1 collagen defect, with multiple fractures following slight trauma and characteristic rapid but distorted healing [4].
problems.presentation: Affected teeth have an opalescent brown or blue hue with bulbous crowns, short roots, and narrow flame-shaped pulps [5]. The amelo-dentinal junction is abnormal, which results in the enamel flaking off and leading to rapid wear of the soft underlying dentine [5]. Children with opalescent teeth may also have brittle bone disease [6].
problems.results: Radiographs reveal bulbous crowns, short roots, and narrow or obliterated pulp chambers — the flame-shaped pulp pattern is characteristic [5]. If Type I is suspected, look for features of osteogenesis imperfecta: history of fractures following slight trauma, blue sclera, and deafness [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The opalescent brown or blue hue combined with rapid enamel chipping and dentine wear, and the radiographic narrow flame-shaped pulp, distinguish dentinogenesis imperfecta from amelogenesis imperfecta (enamel deficient, dentine normal) and tetracycline staining (uniform banding, not opalescent) [5]. The association with osteogenesis imperfecta in Type I adds a systemic dimension [4].
problems.treatment: Seek specialist input. Management follows similar lines to severe amelogenesis imperfecta [5]. Early recognition and treatment is important to prevent rapid tooth wear [7]. Protective restorations and crowns are the mainstay. If osteogenesis imperfecta is suspected, medical referral is needed.
problems.prognosis: Without early protective restorations, rapid and severe tooth wear leads to loss of vertical dimension and extensive dentine exposure [7]. Early and sustained specialist restorative management significantly improves the long-term outcome.

citations.quote: This is more common, affecting 1 in 8000. Both 1° and 2° dentitions are involved, although later-formed teeth may be less so.
I—associated with osteogenesis imperfecta.
II—teeth only.

An autosomal dominant type 1 collagen defect. Multiple # following slight trauma with rapid but distorted healing is characteristic. Associated with blue sclera, deafness, and dentinogenesis imperfecta.

Affected teeth have an opalescent brown or blue hue, bulbous crowns, short roots, and narrow flame-shaped pulps. The ADJ is abnormal, which results in the enamel flaking off, leading to rapid wear of the soft dentine. Rx: along similar lines as for severe amelogenesis.
Children with opalescent teeth may also have brittle bone disease.
Early recognition and Rx of amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta is important to prevent rapid tooth wear.

problems.description: Excessive cementum found around the root of a tooth, making the root bulbous — an incidental finding on a periapical or panoramic radiograph.
problems.etiology: Hypercementosis is relatively common and may occur in response to inflammation, mechanical stimulation, or Paget's disease, or be idiopathic [1]. The root becomes enlarged by excess cementum deposition. Concrescence — the uniting of the roots of two adjacent teeth by cementum — is a related finding [1].
problems.presentation: Usually an incidental radiographic finding with no symptoms from the hypercementosis itself. Occasionally the affected tooth may be difficult to extract because the bulbous root is locked into the socket.
problems.results: Periapical or panoramic radiograph shows the bulbous root enlargement with excess cementum [1]. Vitality testing is positive — hypercementosis does not affect pulp status. Concrescence may be identified when roots of adjacent teeth appear fused.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Hypercementosis is a radiographic diagnosis. The root outline extends beyond the normal taper, with a smooth, rounded enlargement [1]. In the context of Paget's disease, it appears alongside other bony changes [1]. Concrescence means the two affected teeth cannot be moved independently — a practical consequence for both orthodontics and extraction [1].
problems.treatment: No treatment required for hypercementosis itself [1]. The clinical consequence is that extraction may be more complex — warn the patient and plan for potential difficulty, especially if surgical extraction is anticipated.
problems.prognosis: Hypercementosis is a benign finding. Concrescence of adjacent teeth means extraction of one may risk the other [1].

citations.quote: Hypoplasia and aplasia of cementum are uncommon. The latter occurs in hypophosphatasia and results in premature exfoliation. Hypercementosis is relatively common and may occur in response to inflammation, mechanical stimulation, or Paget's disease, or be idiopathic. Concrescence is the uniting of the roots of two teeth by cementum.

problems.description: A tooth that looks like there's a tooth within a tooth — a deep invagination of the enamel on the palatal surface — typically on an upper lateral incisor.
problems.etiology: A marked palatal invagination that gives the appearance of a tooth within a tooth [1]. Usually affects upper lateral incisors but can also affect premolars [1]. Where the invagination is in close proximity to the pulp, early pulp death may follow [1].
problems.presentation: The tooth often looks anatomically unusual — a deep pit on the palatal surface. The patient may be asymptomatic until the pulp becomes non-vital, at which point pain or a sinus may develop. The condition is often found on routine radiographs.
problems.results: Periapical radiograph shows the characteristic tooth-within-a-tooth appearance [1]. Vitality testing may be positive initially but can turn negative if the invagination has led to pulp necrosis. The radiographic appearance is usually diagnostic [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The radiographic tooth-within-a-tooth image is the key finding [1]. The deep palatal pit is the visual clue on examination. The reason it leads to pulp death is the close proximity of the invaginated enamel to the pulp chamber — infection can enter through the pit and track directly to the pulp [1].
problems.treatment: Fissure sealing of the invagination as soon as possible after eruption may prevent pulp death, but is often too late by the time the tooth is seen [1]. If the pulp is still vital, seal or restore the pit. If pulp death has already occurred: RCT (which can be difficult due to the abnormal anatomy), pulpotomy, apical surgery, or extraction [1].
problems.prognosis: Teeth with dens invaginatus have a guarded long-term prognosis because of the risk of early pulp necrosis. If the invagination is sealed promptly after eruption, pulp survival is possible. Once pulp death has occurred, endodontic treatment is technically demanding and outcomes variable [1].

citations.quote: This is really a marked palatal invagination, which gives the appearance of a tooth within a tooth. Usually affects 2s, but can also affect premolars. Where the invagination is in close proximity to the pulp, early pulp death may ensue. Fissure sealing of the invagination as soon as possible after eruption may prevent this, but is often too late. Extraction may be required, other options include RCT (can be difficult), pulpotomy, and apical Rx.

problems.description: A permanent tooth with a distorted crown or root — typically an upper central incisor — where the distortion was caused by trauma to the overlying primary tooth in early childhood.
problems.etiology: Dilaceration describes a tooth with a distorted crown or root [1]. It usually affects upper central incisors [1]. The traumatically induced type is caused by intrusion of the primary incisor, resulting in displacement of the developing permanent tooth germ [2]. The effects depend upon the developmental stage at the time of injury [2].
problems.presentation: The affected tooth may fail to erupt in its normal position, or may erupt with a visibly abnormal crown or root angulation. Parents or patients may notice the tooth is missing, erupting in the wrong place, or has an unusual shape. History of a traumatic fall in the primary dentition years earlier is common.
problems.results: Periapical or panoramic radiograph demonstrates the distorted root or crown form [1]. The relationship of the distorted apex to the labial plate of bone is a key planning factor [3]. Vitality testing on an erupted dilacerated tooth reflects the pulp status, not the morphological distortion.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The link between a primary tooth trauma and the morphological distortion of the permanent successor is the defining clinical narrative [2]. Unlike fusion or gemination (which involve two tooth germs), dilaceration affects a single tooth germ displaced by trauma at a specific developmental moment [1][2].
problems.treatment: Treatment depends on severity and patient cooperation [3]. If mild, expose the crown and align orthodontically — provided the apex will not be positioned against the labial plate of bone at the end of treatment; otherwise extraction is indicated [3].
problems.prognosis: Mild cases treated orthodontically can be aligned successfully provided the root form allows movement [3]. If the apex is positioned unfavourably relative to the labial plate, orthodontic alignment risks labial bone loss and extraction becomes the preferred option [3].

citations.quote: This describes a tooth with a distorted crown or root. Usually affects 1s. Two types seen, dependent upon aetiology (Table 3.3).

The traumatically induced type is caused by intrusion of the 1° incisor, resulting in displacement of the developing 2° incisor tooth germ. The effects depend upon the developmental stage at the time of injury.

Rx: depends upon severity and patient cooperation. If mild it may be possible to expose crown and align orthodontically provided the apex will not be positioned against the labial plate of bone at the end of the Rx, otherwise extraction is indicated.

problems.description: A hypoplastic or discoloured defect on a premolar caused by infection from the overlying primary molar — the developing permanent tooth was damaged by the primary tooth's periapical infection.
problems.etiology: The term describes the effect of a disturbance of enamel and dentine formation caused by infection from an overlying primary tooth [1]. It therefore usually affects premolar teeth, because these develop under primary molars prone to periapical infection in children [1].
problems.presentation: A single premolar (or occasionally another permanent tooth) presents with a localised area of enamel hypoplasia — pitting, discolouration, or structural deficiency on the crown. The rest of the dentition is normal. History often reveals a chronically infected or abscessed primary molar in the corresponding position.
problems.results: Clinical examination identifies the isolated defect on the affected tooth. Vitality testing is positive unless secondary caries has developed. Periapical radiograph may confirm the permanent tooth erupted with the defect and reveal any residual effects of the primary infection.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Turner tooth is almost always a single isolated tooth affected, and the localised nature is the key distinguishing feature from systemic causes of hypoplasia. The primary tooth infection is the mechanism [1]. Unlike chronological hypoplasia, only one tooth in a specific position is affected [1].
problems.treatment: Treatment follows the principles of hypoplasia management [1]: small defects can be fissure-sealed or restored with composite; more extensive defects may need a full coverage crown.
problems.prognosis: The defect is fixed and does not progress once the tooth has erupted. With appropriate restorative management the tooth can be maintained. Secondary caries in the deficient enamel is the main ongoing risk.

citations.quote: This term is used to describe the effect of a disturbance of enamel and dentine formation by infection from an overlying 1° tooth which therefore usually affects premolar teeth. Rx: as for hypoplasia.

problems.description: Diffuse grey-blue or brown banding across multiple teeth — present since childhood, not related to any current pathology — with a history of tetracycline use during tooth development.
problems.etiology: Tetracycline is incorporated during tooth formation, producing a structural pigmentation of the dental hard tissues [1]. This is intrinsic staining — pigment is incorporated during formation rather than diffusing in post-eruption [1]. All teeth forming during the period of exposure are affected.
problems.presentation: Diffuse grey-blue or brown banding across teeth formed during the period of tetracycline exposure. The staining is uniform within a band and matches the incremental lines of enamel formation. No pain, no structural deficiency. The patient is concerned about the cosmetic appearance.
problems.results: Clinical examination identifies the characteristic banding pattern. The stain is intrinsic and cannot be removed by scaling or polishing. Vitality is normal. Radiographic appearance is unremarkable.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The intrinsic nature of the stain and the banding pattern across teeth formed at the same time are the defining features [1]. Unlike extrinsic staining, tetracycline staining is incorporated into the dental hard tissue structure and cannot be scaled away [1]. The history of tetracycline exposure during tooth formation confirms the diagnosis.
problems.treatment: External bleaching with carbamide peroxide in custom trays can give partial improvement for vital tetracycline-stained teeth. Veneers or crowns may be required for severe cases where bleaching is insufficient. Non-vital bleaching (walking bleach) addresses individual discoloured non-vital teeth [2].
problems.prognosis: Tetracycline staining is permanent without restorative intervention. Bleaching gives partial improvement at best in moderate-to-severe cases. Veneers and crowns can mask the discolouration effectively at the cost of tooth preparation.

citations.quote: Incorporation of pigments during tooth formation, e.g. tetracycline staining (blue/brown), porphyria (red).
Diffusion of pigment into hard tissues after formation, e.g. pulp necrosis products (grey), root canal medicaments (grey).

problems.description: A previously root-canal-treated tooth has turned grey or dark, and the patient wants it lightened without a crown.
problems.etiology: Pulp necrosis products and root canal medicaments both diffuse into dentinal tubules and cause grey discolouration of the crown [1]. The walking bleach technique provides a conservative alternative to a post-retained crown for managing this cosmetic problem [2].
problems.presentation: The tooth is visibly darker than its neighbours — typically grey, with depth of discolouration varying based on how long the pulp was non-vital and whether pigmented medicaments were used. No pain, no swelling. The tooth is already root-canal-treated.
problems.results: Clinical examination confirms the discolouration and the existing root-canal treatment. Periapical radiograph checks the adequacy of the root filling and periapical status before proceeding with internal bleaching. Vitality testing confirms non-vital status.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The discolouration of a root-filled tooth is intrinsic — it cannot be removed with external bleaching alone. The interesting bit is that the degree and duration of discolouration and the age of the patient do not affect the prognosis for a successful result [2]. The walking bleach technique works from inside the access cavity; vital bleaching works from outside.
problems.treatment: Here's the sequence for the walking bleach technique: place Orabase around the gingivae and isolate with rubber dam [3]. Open the access cavity and remove root filling to 2 mm below the gingival margin — a periodontal probe is a useful guide [4]. Place a thin layer of glass ionomer over the root filling to prevent root resorption [5]. Remove any stained dentine within the pulp chamber [6]. Clean access cavity with etchant on a pledget of cotton wool, repeat with alcohol, wash and dry [7]. Place 35% carbamide peroxide [8]. Seal with a pledget of cotton wool and glass ionomer [9]. Review after 1–2 weeks and repeat up to twice if needed [10]. Seal the access cavity permanently with a light shade of resin composite [11]. Warn the patient that there is a tendency for discolouration to recur over time — over-bleach to account for this [2].
problems.prognosis: The technique usually achieves an improvement in shade rather than a perfect result [2]. Discolouration may recur over time [2]. If internal bleaching is insufficient, a veneer or crown is the next option.

citations.quote: Diffusion of pigment into hard tissues after formation, e.g. pulp necrosis products (grey), root canal medicaments (grey).

This provides a conservative alternative to a post-retained crown for the discoloured root-filled tooth. However, it usually only achieves an improvement in shade. There is a tendency for the discoloration to recur over time, therefore warn the patient and over-bleach. Interestingly, it has been shown that the degree and duration of discoloration and the age of the patient do not affect the prognosis for a successful result.
Place Orabase® around gingivae of tooth to be treated and isolate with rubber dam.
Open access cavity and remove root filling to 2mm below gingival margin (a perio probe is a useful guide).
Place thin layer of GI over root filling to prevent root resorption.
Remove any stained dentine within pulp chamber.
Clean access cavity with etchant on a pledget of cotton wool and then repeat with alcohol. Wash and dry.
Place 35% carbamide peroxide.

Review after 1–2 weeks and repeat (up to 2×) if necessary.
Seal access cavity permanently with a light shade of resin composite.

problems.description: A patient undergoing home tooth whitening notices sharp sensitivity during or shortly after tray application.
problems.etiology: Whitening with carbamide or hydrogen peroxide products is safe and effective when used correctly [1]. The recognised potential local adverse effects include gingival irritation and tooth sensitivity [1]. Some shade rebound may occur shortly after treatment [1].
problems.presentation: Sensitivity is typically sharp and elicited by cold or air exposure during or shortly after whitening tray use. It may occur on multiple teeth simultaneously. It is transient and linked temporally to whitening episodes rather than representing a new pathological process.
problems.results: Clinical examination typically reveals no objective findings. Vitality testing is positive. No radiographic changes. The diagnosis is from the history of whitening treatment.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The temporal link to whitening use distinguishes this from other causes of tooth sensitivity [1]. Sensitivity resolves when whitening is paused. Under the current European Directive, products containing or releasing between 0.1% and 6% hydrogen peroxide cannot be used on anyone under 18 years of age [2], and must only be used after appropriate clinical examination to ensure no risk factors or oral pathology concerns are present [3].
problems.treatment: The goal is to manage the sensitivity while completing the whitening course. Pause treatment if sensitivity is severe. Use desensitising toothpaste during and after whitening. Reduce tray wear time or concentration if possible. Products must only be used by or under the direct supervision of a regulated dental professional [4].
problems.prognosis: Tooth sensitivity following whitening is transient and self-limiting once whitening is stopped or reduced [1]. Some shade rebound is expected after completion [1].

citations.quote: Tooth whitening (bleaching) provides a non-invasive solution for mild to moderately discoloured vital or root-filled teeth. It is safe and effective provided it is used properly. Potential local adverse effects include gingival irritation and tooth sensitivity. Some shade rebound may occur shortly after Rx.
Products containing or releasing between 0.1% and 6% hydrogen peroxide cannot be used on any person under 18yrs of age.
Products containing between 0.1% and 6% hydrogen peroxide should only be used after appropriate clinical examination to ensure there are no risk factors or oral pathology concerns.
Whitening is the practice of dentistry and that it should only be undertaken by regulated dental professionals.

problems.description: Cervical resorption lesions develop on a root-filled tooth following internal bleaching — a pink spot near the gum, or an incidental radiographic finding of root surface loss.
problems.etiology: Thermocatalytic bleaching techniques — where the hydrogen peroxide is heated within the pulp chamber — are associated with the development of cervical resorption lesions [1]. This is why thermocatalytic techniques should no longer be used [1].
problems.presentation: Cervical resorption may present as a pink spot visible through the enamel at the cervical margin, or may be an incidental radiographic finding. The affected tooth is non-vital and root-filled. The lesion is at the cervical root level.
problems.results: Periapical radiograph shows the resorptive defect at the cervical root level. A glass ionomer barrier placed over the root filling at 2 mm below the gingival margin during the walking bleach technique is specifically intended to protect the root surface and prevent this complication [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The specific association with thermocatalytic bleaching technique is the defining feature [1]. This is an iatrogenic complication of heating hydrogen peroxide in the pulp chamber — a risk that the walking bleach technique (without heat) eliminates [1].
problems.treatment: Thermocatalytic techniques should no longer be used [1]. For the walking bleach technique, place a thin layer of glass ionomer over the root filling at 2 mm below the gingival margin before placing the bleaching agent — this barrier prevents root resorption [2].
problems.prognosis: Established cervical resorption lesions require specialist management. Prevention is the key: avoiding thermocatalytic bleaching eliminates this particular risk entirely [1].

citations.quote: Thermocatalytic techniques, where the hydrogen peroxide is heated within the pulp chamber, should no longer be used, as they are associated with the development of cervical resorption lesions.
Place thin layer of GI over root filling to prevent root resorption.

problems.description: A white spot or opacity on the enamel surface — post-orthodontic, fluorosis-related, or from a localised developmental insult — where the discolouration is limited to the outer enamel layer.
problems.conditionName: Localised enamel white-spot lesion (post-orthodontic / fluorosis / localised hypoplasia)
problems.etiology: White-spot lesions with discolouration limited to the outer enamel layer are amenable to microabrasion regardless of their origin [1]. Post-orthodontic demineralisation forms at bracket margins when oral hygiene is poor during treatment. Fluorosis produces bilateral symmetrical mottling as previously described. Localised hypoplasia from infection or trauma produces isolated white or discoloured areas.
problems.presentation: A visible white or opaque area on the enamel surface, not cavitated, with tooth structure otherwise intact. The patient is concerned about the cosmetic appearance. No pain unless the surface is rough and trapping plaque.
problems.results: Clinical examination confirms the enamel surface is intact and the discolouration appears limited to the outer enamel. Vitality is normal. The question is whether the discolouration is limited to the outer enamel layer — this determines whether microabrasion is appropriate [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The key diagnostic question is whether discolouration is limited to the outer enamel layer, making it accessible to microabrasion [1]. Post-orthodontic demineralisation is typically at the bracket outline on the buccal surface; fluorosis is bilateral and symmetrical; localised hypoplasia follows a specific traumatic or infectious event.
problems.treatment: Microabrasion is the treatment of choice when discolouration is limited to the outer enamel layer [1]. Carefully isolate, clean, and dry the affected teeth. Polish with a slurry of phosphoric acid mixed with pumice, or a commercially available microabrasion product (usually based on hydrochloric acid) [1]. Review at 1–4 weeks once teeth have rehydrated and photograph the result [1].
problems.prognosis: Microabrasion gives good cosmetic results for outer-enamel discolouration, reviewed after rehydration [1]. If the lesion is deeper than the outer enamel, microabrasion will not fully resolve it — a composite veneer or bonding may then be required.

citations.quote: This is indicated for fluorosis, post-orthodontic demineralization, localized hypoplasia due to infection or trauma, and idiopathic hypoplasia where discoloration is limited to the outer enamel layer. Affected teeth are carefully isolated, cleaned, and dried before 'polishing' the teeth with a slurry of either phosphoric acid (etch) mixed with pumice or a similar commercially available product (usually based on hydrochloric acid). Teeth treated in this way should be reviewed at 1–4 weeks for effect once teeth have re-hydrated and photographs taken.

problems.description: A tooth with an unusually large pulp chamber that looks like a bull's head on the radiograph — the root is short relative to the elongated pulp space.
problems.etiology: Taurodontism means 'bull-like' [1]. It may occur in some types of amelogenesis imperfecta [1]. The pulp chamber is elongated apically, producing the characteristic radiographic appearance [1].
problems.presentation: Usually an incidental radiographic finding. The tooth has a normal clinical appearance. No symptoms arise from taurodontism itself.
problems.results: Radiograph shows the elongated pulp chamber that resembles a bull's head [1]. The root portion is correspondingly shorter relative to the crown. Vitality testing is positive unless there is unrelated pulp pathology.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The radiographic appearance is the diagnostic hallmark: the pulp chamber extends apically into the root portion of the tooth in a way that resembles a bull's head on X-ray [1]. The condition has no clinical symptoms of its own.
problems.treatment: No treatment is required for taurodontism itself [1]. The practical consequence is that the abnormal pulp chamber anatomy may complicate endodontic treatment or occasionally extraction — this needs to be anticipated before starting these procedures [1].
problems.prognosis: The condition is benign. The main practical implication is procedural difficulty if RCT or extraction is needed [1].

citations.quote: Taurodontism means 'bull-like'. May occur in some types of AI. Radiographically an elongation of the pulp chamber is seen, which resembles a bull's head. Rx: none required, but may complicate endodontic Rx and occasionally extraction.

problems.description: Upper permanent incisors with a notched, peg-shaped form, and first permanent molars with a mulberry-like occlusal surface — in a patient with features of a congenital infection.
problems.conditionName: Congenital syphilis (Hutchinson incisors and mulberry molars)
problems.etiology: Due to Treponema pallidum crossing the placental barrier during maternal syphilis [1]. The resulting systemic infection during tooth development produces the classical features: Hutchinson incisors (peg-shaped with a notch at the incisal edge) and mulberry (Moon) molars, alongside saddle nose, frontal bossing, and sensorineural deafness [1].
problems.presentation: Hutchinson incisors are peg-shaped with a notch at the incisal edge [1]. Mulberry molars have a knobbed, mulberry-like occlusal surface [1]. The patient may have the other systemic stigmata of congenital syphilis: saddle nose, frontal bossing, and sensorineural deafness [1].
problems.results: Clinical examination identifies the characteristic tooth morphology. Serological testing confirms the diagnosis systemically. The dental findings are part of a broader syndromic picture.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of Hutchinson incisors and mulberry molars is pathognomonic for congenital syphilis among developmental dental anomalies [1]. The broader facial and systemic features confirm the syndromic context [1].
problems.treatment: The dental management addresses the morphological consequences: notched incisors and irregular molars may require restoration, build-up, or crowning for function and aesthetics. Systemic medical management is the primary treatment for the underlying infection.
problems.prognosis: The dental morphological changes are permanent and fixed at eruption. Management is restorative and symptomatic. Systemic prognosis depends on the underlying syphilis treatment.

citations.quote: Due to T. pallidum crossing the placental barrier leading to the classical appearance of saddle nose, frontal bossing, sensorineural deafness, Hutchinson incisors (peg-shaped with notch), and mulberry (Moon) molars.

problems.description: A chip off a front tooth after a knock, exposing yellow dentine beneath the broken enamel edge — sensitive to cold air or touch but the pulp is still intact.
problems.conditionName: Crown fracture involving enamel and dentine (uncomplicated)
problems.etiology: Trauma exposes dentine directly. The reason sensitivity follows is that the dentinal tubules are now open to oral fluids, creating hydrodynamic stimulation of pulpal fibres [1]. The pulp itself is not breached, but it is at risk if the exposure is deep and close to the pulp horns.
problems.presentation: History of a blow to the tooth, usually a central incisor. The patient reports cold sensitivity and sometimes sharp pain on air contact. Visually, enamel and exposed yellow dentine are visible at the fracture surface [1].
problems.results: Vitality testing is positive. Percussion is not tender unless there is concurrent subluxation. Radiograph: check for root fracture at two angulations. The fracture itself is visible clinically; radiograph confirms root status.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The fracture involves enamel and dentine but the pulp is not exposed — no pink blush or bleeding at the fracture site. If the fracture is near the pulp, treat as for pulp involvement [1].
problems.treatment: The goal is to protect exposed dentine and restore crown contour. Cover exposed dentine with hard-setting calcium hydroxide cement and place an acid-etch retained composite tip using a cellulose acetate crown former as a guide [1]. If time is short, a temporary cover with GIC is acceptable. Keep under review. A veneer or porcelain jacket crown can be considered later [1].
problems.prognosis: Good provided dentine is sealed promptly and vitality maintained. Pulp may become non-vital later — keep under long-term review.

citations.quote: Need to protect exposed dentine, preferably with a hard-setting calcium hydroxide cement and an acid-etch retained composite. If time permits, this can be done with a crown former to restore tooth contour. Keep under review. Veneer or porcelain jacket crown (PJC) can be considered later. If # near to pulp, treat as for pulp involvement.

problems.description: A fractured front tooth after a blow where the break has reached the pulp — a small pink or bleeding spot is visible at the fracture surface.
problems.conditionName: Crown fracture with pulp exposure (complicated crown fracture)
problems.etiology: Trauma exposes the pulp directly. What happens next depends on how much time has passed since injury, how large the exposure is, and whether root development is complete [1]. An open apex means a richer blood supply to the pulp, which improves the chance of keeping the radicular pulp alive and allowing root closure to continue [1].
problems.presentation: History of dental trauma. The patient may report bleeding from the tooth or a visible pink spot at the fracture surface. Sensitivity to cold and touch is expected. Associated injuries to the supporting tissues may be present.
problems.results: Vitality testing should still be positive if carried out promptly after injury — loss of response may indicate concurrent pulp death from vascular disruption rather than the exposure itself [1]. Two radiographic views at different vertical angulations are needed to exclude concurrent root fracture [1]. Root development status (open vs closed apex) is the key radiographic finding driving treatment choice.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Complicated crown fracture means pulp breach — a pink blush or frank blood at the fracture surface distinguishes this from an uncomplicated enamel-dentine fracture. Management pivots entirely on root development status and time since injury [1].
problems.treatment:
Here's the sequence, determined by root development and exposure size [1]:

- **Pulp cap** (exposure <1 mm, <24 h, pulp vital, any root stage): cover with calcium hydroxide (e.g. Dycal®) and composite tip. Review vitality [1].
- **Partial (Cvek) pulpotomy** (exposure >1 mm, >24 h, pulp vital, any root stage): LA and rubber dam. Enlarge access at exposure site with a high-speed bur, amputate pulp 2–4 mm into healthy tissue, arrest bleeding with sterile moist cotton wool (several minutes), cover with non-setting calcium hydroxide, seal with GIC, restore crown [1].
- **Full coronal pulpotomy** (large or contaminated exposure, long duration, incomplete root development, impaired coronal vascularity): LA and rubber dam. Open pulp chamber, amputate coronal pulp to cervical constriction, wash with sterile water, place non-setting calcium hydroxide, restore with polycarboxylate or GIC and composite. Review at 6–8 weeks [1].
- If apex is already closed and pulp is non-vital: RCT [1].

All pulpotomised teeth need long-term review — pulp necrosis and calcification are common sequelae [1].
problems.prognosis: Success rates of 72% for cervical pulpotomies and 96% for minimal (Cvek) pulpotomies have been reported [1]. Long-term review is mandatory as pulp necrosis and calcification occur, even after apparently successful treatment [1].

citations.quote: Rx depends upon size of exposure, state of root development (1 root radiographically complete 10–11yrs, histologically 14–15yrs), time since injury, and other injuries (e.g. root #). If apex open, there is an ↑ blood supply to pulp, therefore likelihood of pulp death ↓. This is advantageous as Rx should be directed towards retaining vitality of radicular pulp to allow root closure to continue. Pulp cap: Indications: exposure <1mm; <24h; complete or incomplete root development; pulp still vital. Cover exposure with calcium hydroxide (e.g. Dycal®), and place composite tip. Partial (Cvek) pulpotomy: Indications: exposure >1mm; >24h; complete or incomplete root development, pulp still vital. Full coronal pulpotomy: Indications: large, contaminated exposures; long duration; incomplete root development; coronal pulp demonstrates impaired vascularity. All pulpotomized teeth should be kept under long-term review as pulp necrosis and calcification are common sequelae. Success rates of 72% for cervical pulpotomies and 96% for minimal (Cvek) pulpotomies have been reported.

problems.description: A tooth that was hit hard and is now loose or displaced, with radiographic evidence of a fracture line somewhere along the root — not the crown.
problems.etiology: Root fractures account for fewer than 10% of injuries to the permanent dentition [1]. The prognosis depends on whether the fracture line communicates with the gingival crevice, on the position of the fracture along the root, and on how much the fragments have been displaced [1].
problems.presentation: History of trauma. The tooth may be mobile or slightly displaced. The crown looks intact. Tenderness on biting is common. Gingival bleeding may be present if the fracture is high.
problems.results: Two radiographic views at different vertical angulations are needed to improve the chance of visualising the fracture line [1]. The position along the root (apical third, middle third, coronal third) is the key radiographic finding that drives management. Vitality testing is positive early on; loss of vitality in the coronal two-thirds signals a complication to watch for [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
Three zones, three management paths [1]:

- **Apical third**: usually no treatment needed unless mobility becomes significant. Pulp of the coronal fragment may die — prepare canal only to the fracture line, since the apical third often retains vitality. Prognosis good. If extraction is required, the apical fragment can be left in situ to preserve bone [1].
- **Middle third**: tooth usually loosened — rigid splinting was previously advocated for 12 weeks, but recent evidence supports flexible splinting for 4 weeks with similar outcomes. If coronal fragment is not displaced, loss of vitality is unlikely. If displaced, reposition, splint, and if vitality is lost, RCT to the fracture line using calcium hydroxide as an interim dressing [1].
- **Coronal third**: high risk of communication with the gingival crevice. Where there is no obvious risk, flexible splinting for up to 4 months. Where the fracture extends coronally, emergency options are temporary stabilisation or extraction of the coronal fragment; permanent treatment is usually post and core crown [1].
problems.treatment: Treatment is position-dependent (see defining characteristics). The overarching principle: reposition and splint where possible, using flexible splinting of the minimum duration needed for the fracture position. Calcium hydroxide dressing limits inflammation and resorption in middle-third fractures. For fractures below the alveolar crest, orthodontic extrusion using gentle forces of 50–100 g can improve access for crown fabrication; retain for at least 3–6 months after extrusion before fabricating the permanent restoration [1].
problems.prognosis: Apical-third fractures carry a good prognosis. Middle-third fractures depend on extent of displacement and timely treatment — delay reduces prognosis [1]. Coronal-third fractures carry the highest risk, primarily from bacterial ingress via the gingival crevice. Vertical root fractures usually require extraction [1].

citations.quote: Account for <10% of injuries to permanent dentition. The prognosis for this type of injury depends upon whether the # line communicates with the gingival crevice. Actual Rx depends on position of #. The prognosis is also affected by the degree of dislocation of apical and coronal fragments and mobility/displacement. Apical third: Usually no Rx is required unless mobility ↑ significantly. Middle third: In the majority of cases the tooth is loosened, therefore rigid splinting is advisable. 12 weeks of rigid splinting was previously advocated, but recent evidence suggests flexible splinting for 4 weeks may give a similar outcome. Coronal third: In this group there is a high risk of direct communication with the gingival crevice. An orthodontic extrusion will need either a URA or a sectional FA with an attachment bonded on to the labial surface. Gentle forces of 50–100g should be used. When sufficient extrusion has been achieved, retain for at least 3–6 months before fabricating a permanent restoration.

problems.description: A tooth that was hit but has not moved — it hurts to bite on and is tender to the lightest touch, but it sits exactly where it always has.
problems.conditionName: Concussion and subluxation of permanent tooth
problems.etiology: Concussion is injury to the supporting tissues of the tooth without any displacement [1]. Subluxation is loosening of the tooth without displacement — the PDL fibres are stretched or partially torn but the tooth stays in its socket [1]. The injury is to the periodontal ligament, not the pulp primarily, though pulp death can follow as a late complication.
problems.presentation: History of a blow. The tooth is painful to bite on and tender to percussion. In concussion it sits perfectly in its socket; in subluxation it feels loose to the patient but has not moved from its position [1].
problems.results: Vitality testing is positive at presentation but may become negative weeks later as a late vascular consequence. Percussion is tender. Mobility is normal in concussion; slightly increased in subluxation. Radiograph: no displacement, no root fracture.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The key distinction from luxation injuries is the absence of any displacement. The tooth is in its correct position — it is the supporting structures that are damaged, not the tooth position [1].
problems.treatment: Concussion: reassurance and a soft diet [1]. Subluxation: if minor, soft diet only is needed; if the tooth is mobile, splint for 1–2 weeks and watch vitality [1].
problems.prognosis: Generally good. Pulp survival is high for concussion. Subluxation carries a risk of later vitality loss — keep under long-term review, including periodic vitality testing and periapical radiographs.

citations.quote: Concussion: Injury to supporting tissues of tooth, without displacement. Subluxation: Actually means partial displacement, but commonly used to describe loosening of a tooth without displacement. Rx: Concussion: Reassurance and soft diet. Subluxation: If minor, no Rx other than advising a soft diet is necessary. If mobile, splint for 1–2 weeks and watch vitality.

problems.description: A front tooth that has shifted sideways, labially, or palatally after a blow — it is not in its original position and may be locking the bite.
problems.etiology: Lateral displacement of the tooth labially, buccally, or palatally from the socket, with the PDL torn on one side and the alveolar socket wall often fractured [1]. Lateral luxation injuries occur in 15–40% of all dental injuries [1].
problems.presentation: History of trauma. The tooth is visibly displaced from its original position. It may be locking the occlusion, preventing the patient from closing. The tooth is tender and may be mobile. Gingival laceration often accompanies the displacement.
problems.results: Clinical: tooth is visibly out of position, occlusion often disrupted. Radiograph: two views to assess socket integrity and exclude root fracture. Vitality testing is often negative initially — the thing is, this doesn't necessarily mean permanent pulp death in immature teeth, which have a better chance of pulp survival. Loss of vitality in mature teeth with closed apices is a common sequel, occurring in approximately 70% of cases [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Lateral luxation involves displacement without complete exit from the socket. If the displaced tooth is interfering with the occlusion, a URA with buccal capping should be fitted as soon as possible to protect the bite and allow healing [1].
problems.treatment: Reposition as soon as possible. LA and use fingers to push the tooth back into position [1]. Splint flexibly for 2–3 weeks [1]. If there has been a delay of more than 24 hours, manual reduction is unlikely to succeed — in these cases orthodontic repositioning is the alternative [1]. If the socket is comminuted, extend the splinting period to 6–8 weeks [1].
problems.prognosis: Pulp survival is much better in teeth with immature (open) apices [1]. In mature teeth, loss of vitality occurs in approximately 70%, leading to inflammatory resorption if not managed [1]. External or internal resorption and pulp canal obliteration may also occur — long-term review is essential [1].

citations.quote: Lateral luxation: Displacement of tooth (laterally, labially, or palatally). Need to reposition tooth as soon as possible. Give LA and use fingers to push back into place. Then tooth should be splinted flexibly for 2–3 weeks. If there has been a delay of >24h since the injury, manual reduction is unlikely to be successful. If the displaced tooth is interfering with the occlusion a URA, with buccal capping, should be fitted as soon as possible. If root development is complete, loss of vitality is a common sequelae following luxation (~70%), leading to inflammatory resorption. Teeth with immature apices have a much better chance of pulp survival. External or internal resorption and pulp canal obliteration may also occur, therefore keep under review. Prevalence: 15–40% of injuries.

problems.description: A tooth driven up into the gum after a blow — it appears shorter than its neighbours and is immobile, often ringing solid on percussion.
problems.etiology: Displacement of the tooth into its socket by a force directed along the long axis, often accompanied by fracture of the alveolar bone [1]. Intrusive luxation falls within the 15–40% prevalence band for all luxation-type injuries [1].
problems.presentation: History of axial trauma. The tooth is visibly shortened compared with adjacent teeth. It is immobile and rings solid on percussion (high metallic note), indicating bone contact. The gingiva may be lacerated around the tooth.
problems.results: Radiograph: the tooth appears driven apically. Alveolar bone fracture is common and may be visible. Vitality testing is often negative acutely — pulp death is virtually certain in teeth with closed apices; it occurs in two-thirds of immature teeth [1]. The degree of intrusion measured radiographically drives the management algorithm.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The intrusion depth and apex status determine treatment path [1]:

- **Open apex, any intrusion depth**: passive repositioning, commencing orthodontic repositioning within 3 weeks.
- **Closed apex, <3 mm intrusion**: passive repositioning, commencing orthodontic repositioning within 3 weeks.
- **Closed apex, 3–6 mm intrusion**: consider orthodontic or surgical repositioning.
- **Closed apex, >6 mm intrusion**: surgical repositioning.

Surgically repositioned teeth require flexible splinting for 1–2 weeks [1].
problems.treatment: Follow the UK guideline algorithm above [1]. Early pulp extirpation and placement of calcium hydroxide dressing is advisable because pulp death and root resorption can develop rapidly after injury [1]. Replacement resorption is also a common sequel [1].
problems.prognosis: Guarded, particularly for mature teeth — pulp death is virtually certain with closed apices, and replacement resorption is a recognised complication [1]. Immature teeth with open apices fare better but still require close monitoring.

citations.quote: Intrusive luxation: Displacement of tooth into its socket. Often accompanied by # of alveolar bone. Current UK guidelines advise passive repositioning, with commencement of orthodontic repositioning within 3 weeks for all teeth with open apices and for teeth intruded <3mm with closed apices. For intrusions of 3–6mm in teeth with a closed apex, consider orthodontic or surgical repositioning, and if intrusion exceeds 6mm with a closed apex, surgically reposition. Surgically repositioned teeth require flexible splinting for 1–2 weeks. Pulp death &/or root resorption can ensue rapidly after injury and early pulp extirpation and placement of the calcium hydroxide dressing is advisable. Pulp death is virtually certain in teeth with closed apices, and occurs in two-thirds of immature teeth. Replacement resorption is also a common sequel. Prevalence: 15–40% of injuries.

problems.description: A tooth hanging partly out of its socket after a blow — it appears longer than its neighbours and is mobile.
problems.etiology: Partial displacement of the tooth out of its socket by a force that has partially torn the periodontal ligament [1]. Falls within the 15–40% prevalence of all luxation-type injuries [1].
problems.presentation: History of trauma. The tooth appears elongated, hangs loosely from the socket, and is tender to touch. The patient notices it feels out of position and the bite is off. Gingival laceration may accompany the injury.
problems.results: Clinical: tooth visibly elongated and mobile. Radiograph: increased apical PDL space or slight displacement visible. Vitality testing may be positive or negative acutely — loss of vitality is a common sequel and the tooth should be monitored for signs of resorption or pulp death [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Extrusive luxation is partial exit from the socket, in contrast to intrusive luxation (driven in) or avulsion (complete exit). The tooth is still in the socket but partially displaced outward — it needs repositioning, not reimplantation.
problems.treatment: Reposition under LA with digital pressure and splint for 1–2 weeks [1]. Observe for signs of resorption or pulp death and manage accordingly [1]. If alveolar bone fracture is also present, extend the splinting period to 3–4 weeks; comminuted socket: 6–8 weeks [1].
problems.prognosis: Loss of vitality is a recognised sequel — long-term review is essential [1]. Immature teeth have a better chance of pulp survival than mature teeth.

citations.quote: Extrusive luxation: Partial displacement of tooth from its socket. The affected tooth should be repositioned under LA with digital pressure and splinted for 1–2 weeks. Again, loss of vitality is a common sequel, so the tooth should be observed for any signs of resorption or pulp death. If any of these situations occur in conjunction with # of the alveolar bone, the splinting period should be ↑ to 3–4 weeks to aid bony healing. If, however, the socket is comminuted, splinting may need to be extended to 6–8 weeks.

problems.description: Radiograph of a previously traumatised tooth shows a ballooning expansion of the root canal from within — the canal is widening, not narrowing.
problems.etiology: Internal resorption is associated with chronic pulpal inflammation, which drives resorption of dentine from the pulpal surface inward [1]. It is commonly seen after avulsion, luxation, intrusion, or extrusion [1]. The process is progressive if the inflamed pulp is not removed.
problems.presentation: Usually asymptomatic and detected as an incidental radiographic finding. The patient may report a history of trauma. A pink discolouration of the crown (pink spot) is occasionally visible clinically if the resorption is coronal and the overlying dentine has thinned — this is the resorbing vascular tissue showing through.
problems.results: Radiograph: a radiolucent ballooning enlargement within the root canal outline, visible as a smooth oval or round expansion from inside the root. Loss of the original canal silhouette. If perforation has occurred, an adjacent radiolucency extending through the root wall into the PDL is visible [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Internal resorption is distinguished from external resorption by its location relative to the canal wall: internal is centred on the canal lumen and originates from the pulpal surface, appearing as an ovoid expansion of the canal [1]. The question is: has it perforated? If perforation has occurred, the prognosis is considerably reduced [1].
problems.treatment: The pulp needs to be carefully extirpated — the process is progressive and will not arrest spontaneously [1]. Dress the tooth with calcium hydroxide, which appears to help arrest the resorption [1]. Once the resorption is controlled, a GP filling can be placed [1]. If perforation has occurred, raising a flap, removing granulation tissue, and attempting direct repair are options, though prognosis is reduced [1].
problems.prognosis: Without treatment: progressive, eventually leading to root perforation or tooth loss. With prompt pulp extirpation and calcium hydroxide dressing, the resorption can be arrested and the tooth saved. Perforation significantly worsens prognosis [1].

citations.quote: Commonly seen after avulsion, luxation, intrusion, or extrusion. Internal resorption: This is associated with chronic pulpal inflammation, which results in resorption of dentine from the pulpal surface. It is progressive, therefore the pulp needs to be carefully extirpated. Dressing the tooth with calcium hydroxide appears to help arrest the resorption and once controlled, a GP filling may be placed. If perforation has occurred, the prognosis is ↓ considerably. Raising a flap, removal of granulation tissue, and direct repair can be attempted.

problems.description: Radiograph of a traumatised tooth shows loss of the periodontal ligament space and patchy root surface erosion — the root itself appears to be disappearing.
problems.etiology: External resorption originates from outside the root surface, involving the cementum and root dentine. Three types are seen: surface (transient), replacement, and inflammatory [1]. Surface resorption occurs from minor trauma to PDL cells and is usually self-limiting, with affected areas repaired by cementum [1]. Replacement resorption is caused by irreversible damage to the cementum, leading to the absence of vital PDL and replacement of root by bone (ankylosis) [1]. Inflammatory resorption is frequently related to pulp necrosis — it depends on both PDL damage and breakdown products from pulp necrosis diffusing through the dentinal tubules [1].
problems.presentation: Usually asymptomatic until advanced. A high percussion note suggests ankylosis from replacement resorption. History of trauma — avulsion, intrusion, or replantation is typical [1].
problems.results: Radiograph: external resorption shows loss of PDL space with no radiolucent areas visible in the replacement type (bone merging with root). Inflammatory type shows irregular pits on the root surface with adjacent radiolucency [1]. In replacement resorption the root is progressively replaced by bone.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The three subtypes have distinct radiographic appearances and clinical implications [1]:

- **Surface resorption**: minor, self-limiting, repaired by cementum. No treatment needed [1].
- **Replacement resorption**: PDL loss, ankylosis, high percussion note, progressive and not influenced by endodontic therapy [1].
- **Inflammatory resorption**: occurs as early as 1–2 weeks after injury, related to pulp necrosis, and can often be halted by appropriate endodontic management [1].

Internal resorption differs from external in that it is centred on the canal and enlarges it from inside.
problems.treatment: Surface resorption: no treatment [1]. Replacement resorption: no treatment available to arrest it; endodontic therapy does not influence it [1]. Inflammatory resorption: prompt pulp extirpation and calcium hydroxide dressing can arrest it; once arrested, a GP filling can be placed [1].
problems.prognosis: Surface resorption is self-limiting and carries a good prognosis [1]. Replacement resorption is usually progressive — once started it eventually leads to root replacement by bone and tooth loss [1]. Inflammatory resorption, once evident radiographically, has a poor prognosis as it is progressive and treatment is not always successful [1].

citations.quote: External resorption: Radiographically, loss of PDL with no radiolucent areas visible. Three types are seen: surface (transient), replacement, and inflammatory. Replacement resorption is usually 2° to irreversible damage to the cementum, leading to ankylosis (usually associated with a high percussion note). Replacement resorption is usually progressive, is not influenced by endodontic therapy, and eventually leads to the root being replaced by bone. Inflammatory resorption is frequently related to pulp necrosis and can often be halted by appropriate endodontic management. Irregular pits are seen on the root with adjacent radiolucency. Surface resorption: This occurs as a result of minor trauma to PDL cells. Usually is self-limiting and affected areas are repaired by cementum. No Rx.

problems.description: Radiograph of a previously luxated or intruded tooth shows the canal has become completely calcified — it is hard or impossible to locate on X-ray.
problems.etiology: Root canal obliteration occurs in 6–35% of luxation-type injuries [1]. The calcification is a response to the injury rather than a direct sign of pathology — it does not mean the pulp is dead.
problems.presentation: Asymptomatic in most cases. Detected on follow-up radiograph after a trauma episode. The tooth may appear normal clinically, with no discolouration or tenderness.
problems.results: Radiograph: hairline canal or no canal detectable on X-ray [1]. Vitality testing may still be positive — the calcified canal does not automatically equal pulp necrosis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The interesting bit is that obliteration is not in itself an indication for prophylactic endodontic treatment [1]. Pulp necrosis occurs in only 13–16% of cases of canal obliteration [1]. And if RCT is eventually needed — for example if the pulp does later become necrotic — a high success rate of 80% has been reported despite a hairline or undetectable canal [1].
problems.treatment: Prophylactic RCT is not necessary [1]. Keep under review. If signs of pulp necrosis develop (pain, swelling, periapical change), proceed to RCT [1].
problems.prognosis: Most teeth with canal obliteration remain asymptomatic. For the minority that require RCT later, an 80% success rate has been reported despite the challenging canal anatomy [1].

citations.quote: Root canal obliteration: Occurs in 6–35% of luxation-type injuries. Prophylactic endodontic Rx is not necessary as pulp necrosis occurs in only 13–16% of cases. A high rate of success (80%) has been reported for subsequent RCT, despite a hairline or no root canal detectable on X-ray.

problems.description: An upper lateral incisor that is missing — either never erupted or lost, leaving a gap that affects the smile line.
problems.conditionName: Congenitally absent upper lateral incisor (missing upper lateral incisor)
problems.etiology: Upper 2 is congenitally absent in approximately 2% of the population — after third molars, it is one of the most commonly absent teeth in the permanent dentition [1]. Absence of 2 also increases the likelihood of ectopic displacement of the adjacent canine (3), because 3 normally migrates down guided by the distal aspect of 2; when 2 is missing, peg-shaped, or small-rooted, the canine has no guide and is prone to ectopic eruption [1]. Upper 1 is rarely congenitally absent — when it is, trauma or dilaceration are the more likely causes [1].
problems.presentation: Gap where the upper lateral incisor should be, or the tooth is present but peg-shaped. The patient may have a retained primary 2. Missing upper anterior teeth are noticed by the general public more readily than other types of malocclusion [1].
problems.results: Radiograph: confirm congenital absence (no unerupted tooth in the alveolus) and monitor the position of the adjacent upper canine for signs of ectopic displacement [1]. Assess the skeletal relationship, degree of crowding, and the form and colour of adjacent teeth — all of these determine the management path [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Management involves two competing strategies: space closure (move the canine mesially to substitute for the lateral) or space opening (maintain or create space for a prosthetic replacement). Neither is universally superior — the choice depends on skeletal class, crowding, the shape and colour of the canine, and patient preference [1]. Patients in previous studies were more satisfied with space closure than prosthetic replacement, though implants and newer materials may shift this [1].
problems.treatment:
The goal is a functional 3-2-1 smile [1]. Factors to weigh [1]:

- Skeletal relationship — space closure in a Class III case can compromise the incisor relationship.
- Crowding/spacing — in an uncrowded arch, space closure is difficult and requires prolonged retention.
- Colour and form of 3 — if significantly darker or caniform in shape, creating a convincing 2 substitute is difficult.
- Minimum implant space for 2 replacement: 6.5 mm [1].

Options: orthodontic space closure with composite reshaping of 3; implant replacement (not before growth is complete); conventional bridgework; resin-bonded bridge.
problems.prognosis: Depends entirely on the treatment path chosen. Orthodontic space closure, done well, produces high patient satisfaction. When 2 is missing and 3 is ectopic, early monitoring and referral is essential to prevent root resorption of adjacent incisors [1].

citations.quote: 1—rarely congenitally absent; usually lost following trauma or because of dilaceration. 2—congenitally absent in ~2% of population (with ↑ likelihood of displacement 3). May also be lost following trauma. Missing upper anterior teeth are noticed by the general public before other types of malocclusion. The aim of Rx is to provide a 321|123 smile. The management of missing incisors involves either recovery or maintenance of space for prosthetic replacement, or orthodontic space closure. Previous studies have shown that patients were more satisfied with space closure than prosthetic replacement. NB: 3 migrates down guided by the distal aspect of 2. When 2 is absent, peg-shaped, or small-rooted, it is important to monitor the maxillary canine for signs of ectopic eruption. Minimum width for implant to replace 2 is 6.5mm.

problems.description: A gap between the two upper front teeth that has persisted beyond the eruption of the canines — the patient is self-conscious about it or asking whether it will close.
problems.etiology: A median diastema between the upper central incisors has several possible causes: small teeth in large jaws, absent or peg-shaped upper 2, midline supernumerary tooth, proclination of upper incisors, physiological (from pressure of developing teeth on upper incisor roots, reducing as the canines erupt), or a prominent upper labial fraenum [1]. Prevalence is high in the young but decreases markedly with age: 98% at age 6, 49% at age 11, 7% in 12–18-year-olds [1]. So in a young child, a median diastema is almost always normal and physiological.
problems.presentation: A visible space between 1 and 1. The patient or parent is concerned about aesthetics or whether it will close. A high or fleshy fraenum may be visible. Peg-shaped or absent 2 may be noted.
problems.results: Periapical radiograph: take to exclude a midline supernumerary tooth [1]. Fraenum involvement is associated with: blanching of the incisive papilla when the fraenum is placed under tension; a V-shaped notch in the interdental bone between 1 and 1 on radiograph; and anterior teeth that may be crowded [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
Management depends on whether the canines have erupted [1]:

- **Before canines erupt**: if diastema <3 mm, review after canine eruption as it will probably reduce unaided. If >3 mm, the incisors may need approximation, but roots of 2 are at risk of resorption against the crowns of the erupting 3 — fixed appliances and prolonged retention are needed [1].
- **After canines erupt**: orthodontic closure will require prolonged retention due to high relapse tendency. If fraenum is aetiological, consider fraenectomy — evidence does not indicate whether this should be done before or during appliance treatment [1]. Alternatively, if teeth are narrower than average (1 = 8.5 mm, 2 = 6.5 mm), composite additions or veneers may close the space without orthodontics [1].
problems.treatment: The goal depends on cause. Exclude supernumerary with periapical X-ray first [1]. Then follow the before/after canine eruption pathway. If space is small and teeth of normal width with no other orthodontic need, the option to accept the diastema is legitimate — it is currently fashionable [1].
problems.prognosis: Physiological diastema in the mixed dentition closes spontaneously as the canines erupt in the majority of cases. Orthodontically closed diastemas have a high tendency to relapse — prolonged retention is always required [1].

citations.quote: Prevalence 6yr-olds = 98%, 11yr-olds = 49%, 12–18yr-olds = 7%. Aetiology: Small teeth in large jaws; absent or peg-shaped 2|2; midline $; proclination of ULS; physiological (caused by pressure of developing teeth on upper incisor roots which reduces as 3 erupts), or due to a fraenum. A fraenum contributes to a diastema in a small number of cases and is associated with: Blanching of incisive papilla when fraenum put under tension. Radiographically there is a V-shaped notch in the interdental bone. Before 3 erupted: if diastema <3mm—review after eruption of canines. If >3mm—may need to approximate incisors. After 3 erupted: orthodontic closure will require prolonged retention as has high tendency to relapse. If fraenum an aetiological factor, consider doing a fraenectomy. Alternatively, measure width of 1 and 2, and if they are narrower than average (1 = 8.5mm, 2 = 6.5mm) consider composite additions or veneers. Take a periapical radiograph to exclude presence of a $.

problems.description: A permanent tooth that simply hasn't appeared on time — it is overdue based on the normal eruption sequence or is more than 6 months behind its contralateral counterpart.
problems.conditionName: Failure of eruption / delayed eruption of permanent tooth
problems.etiology: Disruption of the normal eruption sequence, or asymmetry in eruption times of contralateral teeth exceeding 6 months, warrants investigation [1]. Local causes include: congenital absence (most likely for failure of appearance of 2), crowding, retained primary tooth, supernumerary tooth (most likely cause of failure of eruption of 1), crown or root dilaceration, dentigerous cyst, trauma to a primary tooth leading to displacement of the secondary incisor, and abnormal crypt position [1]. General (systemic) causes include hereditary gingival fibromatosis, Down syndrome, Gardner syndrome, hypothyroidism, cleidocranial dysostosis, and rickets [1].
problems.presentation: What you'll see: the tooth is absent from the arch past its expected eruption time, or one tooth is noticeably behind the equivalent on the other side. The patient or parent is concerned about the gap.
problems.results: Radiograph: the key investigation — confirms the tooth is present or absent, identifies position, and reveals any obstructing pathology. Individual variation in eruption times is wide; developmental age is more meaningful than chronological age when assessing delay [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The cause determines treatment [1]:

- Congenital absence: most likely explanation for a missing 2.
- Supernumerary: most likely explanation for failure of eruption of 1.
- Crowding: extraction of the obstructing teeth to allow eruption.
- Retained primary tooth: extract after confirming the permanent successor is present.
- Primary failure of eruption (rare, usually molars): bone resorption occurs above the tooth but it has no eruptive force — extraction is usually the only option [1].
problems.treatment: Remove the cause where identifiable: extract retained primary tooth, supernumerary, or remove obstruction from crypt [1]. For palatally displaced canines, see the specific entry. For primary failure of eruption in molars, refer for specialist advice — extraction is usually the only option [1].
problems.prognosis: Depends on cause. If the tooth is present, in a reasonable position, and the obstruction is removed, eruption usually follows — average time to eruption after exposure and space creation for a supernumerary-obstructed 1 is 18 months [1]. Primary failure of eruption carries a poor prognosis for conservative management.

citations.quote: Disruption of normal eruption sequence and asymmetry in eruption times of contralateral teeth >6 months warrants further investigation. Developmental age is of more importance in assessing delayed eruption than chronological age. General causes: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis, Down syndrome, Gardner syndrome, hypothyroidism, cleidocranial dysostosis, and rickets. Local causes: Congenital absence. Is the most likely cause for failure of appearance of 2. Crowding. Rx: extractions. Retention of 1° tooth. Rx: extraction of 1° tooth. Supernumerary tooth. Is the most likely reason for failure of eruption of 1. Crown or root dilaceration. Dentigerous cyst. Trauma to 1° tooth leading to lateral or apical displacement of 2° incisor. Abnormal position of crypt. 1° failure of eruption usually affects molar teeth. Refer for advice, usually extraction is only option.

problems.description: The upper first permanent molar is sitting against the back of the second primary molar and cannot erupt freely — it is biting into the primary tooth.
problems.conditionName: Ectopic eruption of the upper first permanent molar
problems.etiology: The upper first permanent molar erupts against the distal surface of the second primary molar (E), occurring in 2–5% of children [1]. It is an indication of crowding [1]. The molar is deflected and cannot jump free past the contact point.
problems.presentation: Detected on dental examination or bitewing radiograph, often incidentally. The 6 appears to be impacted against E, with radiographic evidence of resorption of the distal root of E. The patient is usually a young child (6–8 years old).
problems.results: Radiograph: the upper 6 is angled against the distal of E, with visible resorption of the E root if the situation is established. Clinical: E may have an abnormal mobility or be sore.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The self-correction rate is meaningful: in younger patients under 8 years, many self-correct (jump free) [1]. If still present after 4–6 months without self-correction ('hold'), or in older children, the obstruction is unlikely to resolve unaided [1]. This is the point at which an orthodontic separating spring can be placed to allow the 6 to jump free [1].
problems.treatment: For young patients: wait 4–6 months to allow spontaneous self-correction [1]. If it hasn't self-corrected ('hold'), insert an orthodontic separating spring to allow the 6 to jump free [1]. For severe impactions, keep under observation. If E becomes abscessed or the 6 is at risk of caries, extract the primary tooth — the resulting space loss can be managed later as part of the overall orthodontic plan [1].
problems.prognosis: Good in younger patients, where spontaneous self-correction is common. The space loss from extracting E can usually be managed orthodontically when the patient is older [1].

citations.quote: Ectopic eruption of first permanent molars: Most commonly occurs in the upper arch—against the distal of E occurs in 2–5% of children. It is an indication of crowding.
