In younger patients (<8yrs) many self-correct ('jump'). If still present after 4–6 months ('hold') or in older children, insertion of an orthodontic separating spring may allow the 6 to jump free. More severe impactions should be kept under observation. If the E becomes abscessed or the 6 is in danger of becoming carious then the 1° tooth should be extracted. The resulting space loss can be dealt with later as part of the overall orthodontic Rx plan.

problems.description: An upper first permanent molar that is jammed against the primary tooth in front of it and cannot erupt normally.
problems.etiology: Prevalence is 2–6% [1]. The condition is indicative of crowding [1]. Spontaneous disimpaction is rare after age 8 [1].
problems.presentation: Usually found on dental examination or radiograph in a young child. The 6 is absent or partially erupted and clinically impacted against the primary E. The patient may be asymptomatic.
problems.results: Radiograph: the upper 6 is visibly impacted against the distal of E, with possible root resorption of E. The degree of impaction and root development of the 6 are the key radiographic findings.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The interesting bit is the timing threshold: spontaneous disimpaction is rare after 8 years of age [1]. Before that, a conservative approach is reasonable. After 8, active intervention is needed.
problems.treatment: Attempt to dislodge the 6 by tightening a piece of brass wire around the contact point with E over several visits [1]. If that fails, observe, and extract E only if unavoidable — deal with the resulting space loss in the permanent dentition as part of the orthodontic plan [1].
problems.prognosis: With early intervention, the molar can often be freed. Space loss from extracting E is a predictable consequence and needs orthodontic planning in the mixed or permanent dentition [1].

citations.quote: Impacted upper first permanent molars: Prevalence 2–6%. Indicative of crowding. Spontaneous disimpaction rare after 8yrs. Can try dislodging 6 by tightening a piece of brass wire round the contact point with E over several visits. Otherwise just observe, extracting E if unavoidable and dealing with resultant space loss in 2° dentition.

problems.description: An upper incisor root is showing signs of shortening or blunting on radiograph, and the patient has an unerupted or impacted canine in the vicinity.
problems.conditionName: Root resorption from impacted maxillary canine
problems.etiology: Unerupted and impacted canines can cause resorption of adjacent incisor roots [1]. For resorption to occur, a near head-on collision between the canine and the lateral or central incisor root appears to be required [1].
problems.presentation: Usually asymptomatic and detected radiographically, either on a routine panoramic radiograph or on upper anterior periapical films taken to assess an unerupted canine. The patient may or may not be aware that the canine has not erupted.
problems.results: Radiograph: root shortening or blunting of the incisor adjacent to the impacted canine. A parallax technique (two periapical views at different horizontal angulations) localises the canine relative to the incisor. CBCT provides the most accurate assessment of resorption extent when conventional radiographs are equivocal [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The key clinical decision: how extensive is the resorption? [1] If the resorption is detected early and is limited, extraction of the canine may be sufficient to arrest the process and allow the incisor to be maintained. If the resorption is already extensive, removal of the affected incisor may be preferable, thus allowing the canine to erupt into the space [1].
problems.treatment: Seek specialist opinion quickly once detected on a radiograph [1]. Do not delay — the resorption can progress rapidly. Options: extraction of the canine to limit resorption; or if extensive, removal of the affected incisor and orthodontic management of the canine [1].
problems.prognosis: Early detection is the critical factor. Once detected, timely specialist referral prevents further resorption. Extensive resorption of the incisor carries a poor prognosis for the incisor regardless of canine management [1].

citations.quote: Unerupted and impacted canines can cause resorption of incisor roots. For this to occur, a 'head-on' collision between the two seems to be required. If detected on a radiograph, a specialist opinion should be sought, quickly. Extraction of the canine may be necessary to limit resorption, but if extensive, removal of the affected incisor may be preferable, thus allowing the canine to erupt.

problems.description: Multiple teeth are missing from the adult dentition — either never formed, or only a few permanent teeth developed alongside the primary dentition.
problems.etiology: Developmental absence of one or more permanent teeth [1]. Prevalence in the permanent dentition is 3.5–6.5% [1]. In Caucasians the most commonly absent teeth are third molars (25–35%), upper 2 (approximately 2%), and lower 5 (approximately 3%) [1]. Hypodontia is often familial with polygenic inheritance, and is also associated with ectodermal dysplasia and Down syndrome [1]. Affected patients often have smaller than average teeth in the rest of the dentition [1]. Peg-shaped 2 frequently occurs alongside absence of the contralateral 2 [1].
problems.presentation: Missing teeth in the arch that were expected to erupt. The primary predecessor may be retained and functioning well into adulthood. Spacing in the arch where teeth are absent. Smaller or peg-shaped teeth elsewhere in the dentition.
problems.results: Radiograph: confirms absence of tooth germ. Panoramic radiograph is the standard overview, supplemented by periapical views where needed. Bone volume assessment relevant when implants are being considered.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
Management depends on the location and degree of crowding or spacing in the existing dentition [1]:

- **Third molars**: no treatment [1].
- **Upper 2**: see management of missing incisors — space closure vs prosthetic replacement [1].
- **Lower 5**: if crowded, consider extraction of E at around 8 years to allow spontaneous space closure, or later as part of orthodontic treatment. If the arch is well aligned or spaced, preserve E and consider bridgework later — retained Es with no pathology and good root length can sometimes be maintained into adulthood [1].

Children with hypodontia often benefit from specialist multidisciplinary management coordinating paediatric dentistry, restorative, and orthodontic input [1].
problems.treatment: The goal is coordinated planning across the team. No treatment for absent 8s. For other absent teeth, the options are: orthodontic space closure, implants (after growth completion), conventional bridgework, resin-bonded bridgework, or preservation of the retained primary tooth into adulthood where root quality permits [1].
problems.prognosis: Variable and dependent on which teeth are absent, the skeletal pattern, and the overall treatment plan. Well-managed hypodontia with multidisciplinary input achieves functional and aesthetic outcomes across a range of treatment modalities [1].

citations.quote: Hypodontia (oligodontia): Developmental absence of one or more teeth. Prevalence: 1° dentition: 0.1–0.9%, 2° dentition: 3.5–6.5%. In Caucasians most commonly affected teeth are 8 (25–35%), 2 (2%), lower 5 (3%). Affects F > M and is often associated with smaller than average tooth size in remainder of dentition. Peg-shaped 2 often occurs in conjunction with absence of contralateral 2. NB: 3 migrates down guided by the distal aspect of 2. When 2 is absent, peg-shaped, or small-rooted, it is important to monitor the maxillary canine for signs of ectopic eruption. Aetiology: Often familial—polygenic inheritance. Also associated with ectodermal dysplasia and Down syndrome. 5 — If patient is crowded, extraction of E, either at around 8yrs for spontaneous space closure or later. If lower arch is well aligned or spaced, consider preservation of E, and bridgework later. Children with hypodontia will often benefit from specialist/multidisciplinary management.

problems.description: Extra teeth in the mouth that weren't expected — found on radiograph or erupted in front of or behind a normal tooth, often blocking its eruption.
problems.etiology: Supernumerary teeth occur in 0.8% of the primary dentition and 2% of the permanent dentition [1]. They occur most frequently in the premaxillary region and affect males more than females [1]. They are associated with cleidocranial dysostosis and cleft lip and palate [1]. A supernumerary in the primary dentition is followed by one in the permanent dentition in about 50% of cases — so parents should be warned [1]. Theories of aetiology include offshoot of the dental lamina and third dentition [1].
problems.presentation: The patient or parent reports an extra tooth visible in the mouth, or it is found incidentally on radiograph. A common presentation is failure of eruption of an upper central incisor — a supernumerary (mesiodens) is the most likely cause [1]. The extra tooth may be erupted, unerupted, or inverted.
problems.results: Radiograph: panoramic plus periapical views. The supernumerary's position, orientation (upright, inverted), shape (tuberculate, conical, supplemental), and proximity to the roots of adjacent teeth are all relevant. Classify by shape and position (Table 3.2) [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The effect on the dentition determines management [1]:

- **No effect**: if unerupted, radiographic review to exclude cystic change or damage to adjacent teeth (both relatively rare). If erupted, extract [1].
- **Crowding**: extract; if supplemental, extract the tooth with worse crown or root form [1].
- **Displacement** (rotation and/or displacement of adjacent tooth): extraction and fixed appliance, but tendency to relapse [1].
- **Failure of eruption**: extract and ensure sufficient space for the unerupted tooth. May require extractions and orthodontic appliance. Average time to eruption is 18 months after space creation. If after 2 years the tooth still hasn't erupted, conservative exposure and orthodontic traction may be needed [1].
problems.treatment: Extract the supernumerary and create sufficient space for the obstructed tooth to erupt [1]. Where the unerupted tooth fails to erupt despite space, expose and bond an orthodontic attachment for traction [1].
problems.prognosis: With timely removal of the supernumerary, normal eruption usually follows — average 18 months. Prolonged impaction (>2 years after space creation) may require surgical exposure [1].

citations.quote: Hyperdontia: Better known as supernumerary teeth. Prevalence: 1° dentition 0.8%, 2° dentition 2%. Occurs most frequently in premaxillary region. Affects M > F. Associated with cleidocranial dysostosis and CLP. Supernumerary ($) in 1° dentition is followed in about 50% of cases by $ in 2° dentition, so warn parent! Theories include offshoot of dental lamina and third dentition. No effect. If unerupted keep watch. If erupts—extract. Crowding. Rx: extract. Displacement. Rx: extraction of $ and fixed appliance. Failure of eruption. Most likely cause of 1 to fail to erupt. Rx: extract $ and ensure sufficient space. Average time to eruption in these cases is 18 months. If after 2yrs unerupted tooth fails to erupt despite sufficient space, may require conservative exposure and orthodontic traction.

problems.description: The patient has noticeably spaced teeth across the whole arch — not just a single gap, but generalised spacing throughout.
problems.etiology: Generalised spacing arises from either hypodontia or small teeth in relation to jaw size [1]. Hypodontia is associated with small teeth, so the two often co-exist and compound the spacing [1]. Spacing is uncommon in the UK, where crowding is the norm [1].
problems.presentation: Multiple gaps between teeth across the arch. The patient is self-conscious or asking whether the spaces can be closed. Crowding is absent — teeth appear in correct positions but with spaces between them.
problems.results: Radiograph: to confirm the number of teeth present and identify any absent teeth. Tooth size discrepancy can be measured. Assess whether the spacing is due to tooth absence or to tooth size mismatch.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Management of generalised spacing is described as problematic [1]. A purely orthodontic approach is liable to relapse and requires prolonged retention [1]. The decision tree: in milder cases, building up small teeth with composite or veneers — or accepting the spacing — may be wiser than orthodontics. In more severe cases, a combined restorative and orthodontic approach to localise space for prostheses or implants is needed [1].
problems.treatment: The goal is a stable functional and aesthetic result. Mild cases: composite build-ups or veneers to narrow the spaces, or accept the spacing [1]. Severe cases: combined orthodontic and restorative approach to consolidate and localise spaces for implants or bridgework [1].
problems.prognosis: Purely orthodontic closure tends to relapse without indefinite retention. The more durable route in generalised spacing from hypodontia/microdontia is a combined approach integrating restorative treatment [1].

citations.quote: Generalised spacing: This is due either to hypodontia or small teeth &/or large jaws. Note that hypodontia is associated with small teeth. Rx of spacing is problematic; a purely orthodontic approach is liable to relapse and requires prolonged retention. In milder cases, it may be wiser to build up the teeth if small or accept the spacing. In more severe cases, a combined restorative/orthodontic approach to localize space for the provision of prostheses or implants may be required. Spacing: Uncommon in the UK; crowding is the norm.

problems.description: A partially erupted lower back tooth with a gum flap over it that is red, swollen, and painful — often worse when the upper tooth bites down on the flap.
problems.etiology: Pericoronitis is inflammation and infection of the gum flap (operculum) overlying a partially erupted tooth, usually a lower third molar [1]. The operculum is often traumatised by the opposing upper tooth biting down on it, perpetuating the inflammatory cycle [1].
problems.presentation: Pain and swelling around the partially erupted molar. The patient may report difficulty opening the mouth, bad taste, or trismus. The operculum is visibly inflamed, red, and tender. Pus may be expressible from under the flap. The upper 8 may be visible traumatising the flap on biting.
problems.results: Clinical: inflamed operculum, partially erupted tooth, often halitosis. Examine the opposing tooth to identify occlusal trauma. Assess for systemic involvement — temperature, lymphadenopathy, trismus — as indicators of spreading infection. Radiograph: assess position of the lower 8 relative to the ramus, root development, and path of eruption.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Nearly all third molars associated with pericoronitis eventually require removal [1]. The immediate management addresses the infection and removes the traumatic trigger; definitive management addresses the third molar.
problems.treatment: The goal is to resolve the acute episode and plan definitive management. Irrigate under the operculum with saline or chlorhexidine [1]. Remove the opposing upper 8 to eliminate occlusal trauma [1]. Antibiotics if systemic signs are present — the same regimen as for a dental abscess [1]. Definitive: nearly all third molars associated with pericoronitis need removal [1].
problems.prognosis: Pericoronitis recurs unless the third molar is removed. Acute episodes settle with conservative management, but without extraction the condition recurs. Spreading infection from pericoronitis can become a fascial space emergency — watch for trismus, systemic upset, and dysphagia.

citations.quote: Pericoronitis is inflammation and infection of a gum flap (operculum) overlying a partially erupted tooth, usually an 8– often traumatized by an overerupted 8. Rx: involves removal of the opposing 8, irrigation under the operculum with saline or chlorhexidine, and antibiotics (as for abscess) if necessary. Nearly all third molars associated with pericoronitis need removal.

problems.description: Severe, worsening pain in an extraction socket starting 2–4 days after the tooth was removed — worse than the original toothache was, with a visible empty socket.
problems.etiology: Dry socket is osteitis of the socket following tooth removal [1]. It is most common in the mandible after removal of molars, especially lower 8s [1]. Predisposing factors include smoking, surgical trauma, use of local anaesthetic (particularly with vasoconstrictor), previous history of dry socket, bone disease, use of oral contraceptives, and immunodeficiency [1].
problems.presentation: Pain onset typically 2–4 days after extraction [1]. The pain is similar in character but worse than the preceding toothache [1]. The socket looks inflamed, and exposed bone is usually visible [1]. The patient may describe a foul taste.
problems.results: Clinical: empty socket with exposed bone, inflamed surrounding mucosa. Palpation of the socket walls is very tender. No pus is present — this distinguishes it from a socket infection with retained root fragments.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The timing and the exposed bone are the diagnostic keys: pain onset is 2–4 days post-extraction, not immediately after [1]. The socket looks empty and dry with visible bone rather than filled with a normal blood clot [1]. NSAIDs are the systemic analgesic of choice [1].
problems.treatment: Gently irrigate the socket and dress the exposed bone with Alvogyl®, BIPP, or ZOE packs — these provide remarkable analgesia but are difficult to remove [1]. Topical metronidazole is an alternative [1]. Chlorhexidine and/or hot salt mouthwashes may help [1]. NSAIDs are the systemic analgesic of choice [1]. Prophylactic use of anaerobic-targeted antibiotics such as metronidazole reduces the incidence of dry socket [1].
problems.prognosis: Self-limiting condition — bone gradually re-epithelialises over 2–4 weeks. The main impact is patient discomfort in the short term. Dressings provide symptomatic relief while healing occurs [1].

citations.quote: Dry socket is osteitis of a socket following tooth removal. It is commonest in the mandible after removal of molars, especially 8–. Predisposing factors are smoking, surgical trauma, LA, history, bone disease, oral contraceptives, or immunodeficiency. Diagnosis: Pain onset after (usually 2–4 days) extraction, similar in nature but worse than the preceding toothache. The socket looks inflamed and exposed bone is usually visible. Rx is to gently clean the socket by irrigation and dress the exposed bone with Alvogyl®, BIPP, or ZOE packs (provide remarkable analgesia but are a horror to remove). Topical metronidazole is an alternative. Chlorhexidine &/or hot salt mouthwashes may help. NSAIDs are the systemic analgesic of choice. Prophylactic anaerobicidals such as metronidazole reduce the incidence of this condition.

problems.description: A tooth serving as a bridge abutment that has become symptomatic or non-vital — the bridge is still in place but the tooth underneath has died or developed a problem.
problems.conditionName: Loss of vitality of a bridge abutment tooth
problems.etiology: Loss of vitality is a recognised failure mode for fixed bridgework alongside secondary caries, periodontal disease, loss of retention, and mechanical fracture [1]. The abutment tooth is subjected to the biological insult of crown preparation — dentine exposure, heat generation, and the ongoing marginal seal over time.
problems.presentation: The patient may report symptoms developing under an existing bridge: pain on biting, thermal sensitivity, or spontaneous ache. Alternatively, the vitality loss is asymptomatic and detected on routine testing. The bridge itself may appear intact clinically.
problems.results: Vitality testing: negative response over the abutment crown indicates non-vitality. Percussion: the abutment tooth may be TTP if periapical pathology is developing. Radiograph through the retainer: assess for periapical radiolucency, widening of the PDL space, or root resorption. Quality of the marginal seal and crown margins should also be assessed.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The interesting bit is that loss of vitality is not necessarily an indication for bridge removal [1]. RCT can often be carried out through the retainer of the abutment crown [1]. This avoids the trauma and cost of bridge removal and remake — provided access through the retainer is feasible.
problems.treatment: The goal is to preserve the bridge if the failure is localised and manageable [1]. RCT through the retainer of the abutment crown is often possible and avoids bridge removal [1]. Before removing and replacing the bridge, a careful analysis of all reasons for failure is needed — minor problems should be repaired rather than replaced [1]. Secondary caries or marginal deficiencies, if small, can be restored with GIC [1]. Fractured porcelain can be repaired with specialist repair kits such as CoJet™ [1].
problems.prognosis: Depends on the extent of the problem and the feasibility of endodontic access through the retainer. Successful RCT through the retainer allows the bridge to be retained. If the abutment cannot be treated through the retainer, the bridge must be removed — and the question then becomes whether the abutment is restorable at all [1].

citations.quote: Problems with abutment teeth, e.g. 2° caries, periodontal disease, loss of vitality. Before replacement of a bridge is embarked upon, a careful analysis of the reasons for failure is necessary. Minor problems in an otherwise satisfactory bridge should be repaired if at all possible. Fractured porcelain can be repaired with one of the specialized repair kits available (e.g. CoJet™). 2° caries or marginal deficiencies, if small, can be restored with traditional GIC. Failure may be due to loss of vitality. This is not necessarily an indication for removal of the bridge because RCT can often be carried out through the retainer of the abutment.

problems.description: A tooth with a history of trauma or caries shows no visible canal on periapical radiograph. Root canal treatment is now needed because the pulp has died.
problems.etiology: Canal obliteration follows pulpal injury — typically trauma or deep caries — that stimulates tertiary dentine deposition, progressively narrowing and eventually occluding the canal space. The thing is, the pulp doesn't always die: only 13–16% of obliterated canals go on to pulp necrosis [1]. So the canal may be sclerosed without the tooth being in trouble. It only becomes a clinical problem when necrosis does occur and treatment is now needed through calcified tissue.
problems.presentation: The tooth is often asymptomatic until pulp death triggers apical periodontitis. On examination it may be discoloured, with a history of trauma or repeated restorations. The patient presents when the tooth becomes tender to bite on or a sinus appears, at which point the clinician must attempt RCT through calcified tissue.
problems.results: Radiograph shows a canal that appears hairline or is not detectable on the PA. Sensibility testing is negative once pulp is necrotic. Periapical changes (radiolucency, loss of lamina dura) may be present if necrosis has established periapical periodontitis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: What makes this distinct is the combination of a radiographically absent canal and a clinical need for RCT because of pulp necrosis. The question is: can the canal be found? Magnification, illumination, and EDTA lubricants are the tools [1]. Success rates of 80% have been reported even for canals that were hairline or undetectable on radiographs [1].
problems.treatment: Locate the canal orifice with careful exploration using a small file, a small round bur, or ultrasonic tips, aided by magnification and illumination [1]. Once the orifice is found, negotiate with a no. 8 or 10 file using EDTA-containing File-Eze®, Glyde™, or RC Prep™ as lubricant, then prepare and fill conventionally [1]. If a total blockage is encountered, fill to the level reached and consider periradicular surgery [1].
problems.prognosis: Success rates of 80% have been reported for canals that were hairline or undetectable on radiographs [1]. If the canal cannot be negotiated, periradicular surgery is the fallback [1].

citations.quote: As the incidence of pulp necrosis following canal obliteration is only 13–16%, elective RCT is not warranted. However, where pulp death has occurred, finding the canal orifice may be difficult. If careful exploration with a small file is unsuccessful, investigation of the expected position of the canal entrance with a small round bur or ultrasonic tips, aided by magnification and illumination, may help. Once the canal is found, a no. 8 or 10 file should be used to try and negotiate it, using EDTA-containing File-Eze®, Glyde™, or RC Prep™ as a lubricant, and the canal prepared and filled conventionally. Success rates of 80% have been reported for canals that were hairline or undetectable on radiographs. Occasionally, a total blockage of the canal is encountered, in which case the filling is placed to this level &/or periradicular surgery done.

problems.description: Calcified deposits are visible inside the pulp space on radiograph. Encountered during root canal access or investigation of pulpal symptoms.
problems.etiology: Pulp stones are calcified masses within the pulp chamber or root canals. They are a common incidental radiographic finding and are not in themselves a sign of pathology. The clinical significance is practical: they can obstruct access to the root canal orifice during endodontic treatment.
problems.presentation: Usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on bitewing or PA radiograph. Occasionally identified during endodontic access when a file fails to pass the pulp chamber floor. The patient has no symptoms attributable to the pulp stone itself.
problems.results: Radiograph shows radiopaque bodies within the pulp chamber or along the root canal. Sensibility testing reflects the pulpal status independent of the stone. No percussion or palpation tenderness attributable to the stone.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The distinction from canal obliteration is that pulp stones are discrete radio-opaque foci rather than diffuse narrowing. In the chamber they can be dislodged; in the canal they require EDTA and file work [1]. The stone does not itself cause symptoms — the indication for treatment is endodontic disease, not the stone.
problems.treatment: Pulp stones in the pulp chamber can usually be flicked out [1]. If they occur in the canal, use EDTA and a small file to dislodge them [1]. The goal is to clear the obstruction and allow normal canal instrumentation.
problems.prognosis: Once dislodged, the canal can be instrumented and filled normally. No particular adverse prognosis attributable to pulp stones per se.

citations.quote: Pulp stones in the pulp chamber can usually be flicked out. If they occur in the canal, use EDTA and a small file to dislodge them.

problems.description: A file snaps inside the root canal during instrumentation. The broken fragment cannot be removed by simply repeating the filing motion.
problems.etiology: Instrument fracture during root canal preparation is an iatrogenic complication. The outcome depends on root canal anatomy, the type and design of the fractured instrument, and the location of the fractured portion within the canal [1]. A fragment near the apex in a curved canal is the hardest scenario; a coronal fragment in a straight canal is more manageable.
problems.presentation: The clinician notices resistance or loss of length feedback during instrumentation, or discovers the shortened instrument on a check radiograph. The patient has no specific symptoms from the fractured fragment itself. The concern is whether the fragment blocks the canal and prevents adequate debridement.
problems.results: Check radiograph shows a radio-opaque fragment within the canal at a specific level. The location — coronal, middle, or apical third — and the canal curvature together determine the management options [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The fragment may be bypassed without removal in many cases [1]. What makes removal difficult is access: the apical third of a curved canal leaves almost no room to work. So the decision between bypass, attempt at retrieval, obturation short of the fragment, and periradicular surgery as a last resort all hinge on fragment position and canal anatomy [1].
problems.treatment: The fractured file may be bypassed [1]. If retrieval is possible: attempt to pull out with fine Steiglitz forceps [1]. If not, insert a fine file beside the instrument or use ultrasonic tips at low power to create a staging platform and dislodge it [1]. A Masseran kit may be required but these weaken root dentine [1]. If the fragment is in the apical portion, fill the canal coronal to it and keep under observation; resort to periradicular surgery as a last-ditch solution [1].
problems.prognosis: Many fractured instruments can be bypassed or removed. When apically lodged and unremovable, filling coronal to the fragment and observing is a legitimate approach [1]. Periradicular surgery remains available if periapical pathology develops.

citations.quote: The success of removal depends on root canal anatomy and type and design of the # instrument and location of the # portion. The fractured file may be bypassed. Sometimes it is possible to pull out the # portion with a pair of fine Steiglitz forceps. If not, insertion of a fine file beside the instrument or ultrasonic tips to create a staging platform used at a low power setting may dislodge it. Otherwise, a Masseran kit (…… Removing old posts and cores, p. 266) may be required but these weaken the root dentine. Should the # piece be lodged in the apical portion of the canal it may be better to fill the canal coronal to it and keep it under observation, resorting to periradicular surgery as a last-ditch solution.

problems.description: A communication between the root canal and the periodontium or oral cavity occurs during or after root canal treatment, either as an iatrogenic error or due to resorption.
problems.etiology: Perforations can be iatrogenic — from misdirected access or over-preparation — or caused by resorption [1]. The consequences depend on size and position. Small perforations in favourable positions can often be sealed; large or apically placed perforations may require surgery or multirooted tooth modification [1].
problems.presentation: Suspected intra-operatively when there is sudden haemorrhage into the canal not accounted for by pulpal tissue, or post-operatively when periapical symptoms persist or a sinus develops adjacent to the root rather than at the apex. Radiographic confirmation with a file placed to the suspected level establishes the site.
problems.results: Radiograph with a file in situ shows the instrument exiting the canal at a lateral position. Bleeding from a non-pulpal source during access or canal preparation is a key intra-operative signal. Post-operatively, a sinus or periradicular radiolucency at a lateral position rather than the apex points to a perforation.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Location within the canal determines treatment options. Pulp chamber floor perforations — if small — can be covered with MTA or a bioceramic material; if large, hemisection or extraction may be necessary [1]. Lateral perforations near the gingival margin can be incorporated in the final restoration [1]. Middle-third lateral perforations can be managed by passing instruments down the opposite wall and filling with lateral compaction technique [1]. Apical third perforations usually warrant a vertical compaction technique or periradicular surgery [1].
problems.treatment:
For resorption-related perforations: dress with non-setting calcium hydroxide to arrest resorption and promote a calcific barrier [1]. MTA or bioceramic material is the repair material of choice with excellent results [1].

Here's the sequence by location:

- **Pulp chamber floor**: small — cover with MTA or bioceramic; large — consider hemisection or extraction [1].
- **Lateral (gingival margin)**: incorporate in the final restoration [1].
- **Lateral (middle third)**: instrument down the opposite wall, fill with lateral compaction [1]; larger perforations may need a surgical approach [1].
- **Apical third**: attempt vertical compaction to fill both perforation and remainder of canal; if unsuccessful, periradicular surgery [1].
problems.prognosis: MTA repair of perforations carries excellent results [1]. Large or infected perforations in multirooted teeth carry a guarded prognosis and may lead to tooth loss.

citations.quote: These can be iatrogenic or caused by resorption. In the latter case, dressing with non-setting calcium hydroxide may help to arrest the resorption and promote formation of a calcific barrier. Increasingly, MTA is being used for the repair of perforations and in surgical endodontics as a retrograde filling material with excellent results. Management of traumatic perforations depends upon their size and position: Pulp chamber floor—if small, can cover with MTA or a bioceramic material, but if large, hemisection or extraction may be necessary. MTA can also be used. Lateral perforation—if near the gingival margin, can be incorporated in the final restoration, e.g. a diaphragm post and core crown. If in the middle third, the remainder of the canal may be cleaned by passing instruments down the side of the wall opposite the perforation. Then the canal can be filled with GP, using a lateral compaction technique to occlude the perforation as well. Larger perforations may require a surgical approach and in multirooted teeth hemisection or extraction may be unavoidable. Apical third—it is usually worth trying a vertical compaction technique to attempt to fill both the perforation and the remainder of the canal. If this is unsuccessful, periradicular surgery will be required.

problems.description: Symptoms persist or return months to years after root canal treatment that appeared technically adequate at the time.
problems.conditionName: Persistent / recurrent periapical periodontitis after root canal treatment
problems.etiology: Following RCT the ideal outcome is prevention or resolution of periapical periodontitis and absence of clinical signs and symptoms [1]. In some cases, however, periapical periodontitis will persist, develop, or recur [1]. Three factors dominate the outcome: the pre-treatment periapical status, the quality and length of the root canal filling, and the quality of the coronal restoration [2][3].
problems.presentation: The patient returns with tenderness on biting, a persistent or re-appearing sinus, or a periapical radiolucency found on routine follow-up. The tooth was previously root-treated and restored. Symptoms may be subtle — just a low-grade TTP — or may escalate to an acute flare.
problems.results: Radiograph shows a persistent or enlarging periapical radiolucency, or one that fails to show the expected reduction in size at one-year review [1]. Outcome is most favourable — up to 95% — when there was no pre-treatment radiolucency and the RCF is well compacted within 2mm of the radiographic apex [2]. Pre-existing lesions do better when smaller (<5mm) [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The practical framework: absence of clinical signs and symptoms plus a decrease in size of the apical area is acceptable as success [1]. It is more pragmatic now to consider this as tooth survival rather than strict 'success/failure' [1]. What drives reassessment is a lesion that is not reducing, or new symptoms in a previously treated tooth.
problems.treatment: Reassess the three prognostic factors. Options range from monitoring a small asymptomatic lesion, to orthograde re-treatment (removing the old root filling and re-preparing and re-obturating), through to periradicular surgery if orthograde re-treatment is not possible or has already failed. The quality of the coronal restoration must be addressed alongside the endodontics [3].
problems.prognosis: Pre-treatment outcome data: no pre-treatment radiolucency — outcome up to 95% favourable [2]. With a pre-existing lesion, smaller lesions do better [2]. A well-compacted RCF within 2mm of the radiographic apex is the technical target [2]. Quality of coronal restoration is the third determinant [3].

citations.quote: Following RCT the ideal outcome is prevention or resolution of periapical periodontitis and absence of clinical signs and symptoms. In some cases, however, periapical periodontitis will persist, develop, or recur. Previously, the terms ‘success and ‘failure’ were used. It may be more pragmatic to consider that the absence of clinical signs and symptoms and a ↓ in size of any apical area be deemed acceptable. Considering this as tooth survival (having an asymptomatic functional tooth) is more in line with the criteria used to judge the outcome of implant placement.

Pre-treatment status of the periapical tissues—if there is no pre-treatment radiolucency, outcome is more favourable and can be up to 95%. If there is a lesion, outcome is more favourable for smaller (<5mm) lesions. Quality and length of RCF—outcome is more favourable if well compacted and reaches within 2mm of the radiographic apex.
Quality of coronal restoration.

problems.description: A cyst discovered on periapical radiograph at the root apex of a tooth with a necrotic pulp or a previously root-treated tooth.
problems.etiology: Radicular cysts are the commonest type of dental cyst. They are inflammatory dental cysts — the stimulus is a necrotic pulp, and the cyst epithelium comes from cell rests of Malassez in the PDL [1]. They can arise apically, laterally (at a lateral root canal), or as a residual cyst left behind after extraction [1].
problems.presentation: Usually asymptomatic and discovered as an incidental finding on routine periapical or bitewing radiograph. The associated tooth is non-vital. A slow-expanding painless swelling of the jaw may be the first sign if the cyst grows large. An acute episode of pain and swelling can occur if the cyst becomes infected.
problems.results: Radiograph shows a well-defined periapical radiolucency at the root apex of a non-vital tooth. Sensibility testing is negative. The cyst cannot be reliably distinguished from a periapical granuloma on plain radiograph — only histology makes the distinction [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: What sets the radicular cyst apart from other jaw cysts is its strict association with a non-vital tooth [1]. The interesting bit: granulomas and cysts look identical on plain X-ray. The treatment is the same — enucleation plus endodontics or extraction — so the distinction matters for histological understanding more than immediate clinical decision-making [1].
problems.treatment: Enucleation plus endodontics or extraction of the causative tooth [1]. Always submit the cyst lining for histopathology [2].
problems.prognosis: With definitive treatment (enucleation and root canal treatment or extraction), prognosis is good. Recurrence is uncommon when the cyst is fully enucleated.

citations.quote: These are very common, and may also be called radicular cysts. Described as apical or lateral depending on position in relation to tooth root, or residual if left behind after tooth extraction. Necrotic pulp is the stimulus, and the epithelium comes from cell rests of Malassez. Rx: enucleation plus endodontics or extraction.
Always submit cyst lining for histopathology.

problems.description: Multiple small tooth-like structures, or a disorganised mass of dental hard tissues, discovered on radiograph — often associated with failure of eruption of a permanent tooth.
problems.etiology: Odontomes are not true neoplasms. They are malformations of dental hard tissues [1]. Compound odontomes consist of multiple small tooth-like structures in a fibrous sac; complex odontomes are a congealed, irregular mass of dental hard tissue [1]. Both represent developmental errors in tooth morphogenesis rather than neoplastic growth.
problems.presentation: Frequently discovered incidentally on radiograph taken for delayed eruption or routine survey. May prevent eruption of the underlying permanent tooth. Larger lesions can produce painless jaw expansion. The patient has no pain or specific complaint unless an infection has supervened.
problems.results: Radiograph shows the characteristic pattern: multiple small tooth-like opacities (compound) or an irregular calcified mass (complex), usually within the crown-forming area of an unerupted tooth. The surrounding bony margins are well-defined.
problems.definingCharacteristics: These are best regarded and treated as unerupted, malpositioned, or impacted teeth [1]. The clinical approach mirrors dento-alveolar surgery for impacted teeth, not tumour surgery. The key distinction from a neoplasm is the well-defined border and the dental hard-tissue composition.
problems.treatment: Remove using standard dento-alveolar techniques when required [1]. Post-removal, the associated tooth may erupt if conditions allow, or may need surgical exposure and orthodontic traction.
problems.prognosis: Good. After removal of the odontome, prognosis for eruption of the retained tooth depends on the tooth's position and developmental stage at the time of treatment.

citations.quote: These are not true neoplasms, but malformations of dental hard tissues. Classically, they are classified as compound when they are multiple small ‘teeth’ in a fibrous sac, and complex when they are a congealed irregular mass of dental hard tissue. These are best regarded and treated as unerupted, malpositioned, or impacted teeth, and removed using standard dento-alveolar techniques when required (…… Dento-alveolar surgery: removal of unerupted teeth, p. 394).

problems.description: Smooth, cupped-out erosion on the palatal surfaces of upper front teeth in a young woman. No obvious dietary source of acid. Possible history of vomiting or weight concerns.
problems.conditionName: Perimolysis / tooth erosion in eating disorder (anorexia nervosa / bulimia nervosa)
problems.etiology: Binge-eating followed by vomiting or laxative abuse is the mechanism in bulimia nervosa [1]. Repeated exposure of tooth surfaces to gastric acid produces the erosion pattern. Bingeing without weight loss is bulimia nervosa; anorexia nervosa additionally involves weight loss of more than 25% of ideal body weight and obsessive food avoidance [1]. Both have significant medical implications beyond dentistry.
problems.presentation: Palatal erosion of upper incisors is the characteristic dental finding — gastric acid bathes the palatal surfaces of upper teeth during vomiting. The patient may not volunteer a history of vomiting, and the eating disorder may not yet be diagnosed. Questioning must be sensitive. The interesting bit: this presentation may be the first clinical alert to an underlying eating disorder.
problems.results: Smooth perimolysis-pattern erosion — cupped surfaces, palatal tooth loss, exposed dentine, proud amalgam restorations relative to the eroded enamel. Hypersensitivity may be reported. The intrinsic acid pattern affects palatal surfaces of upper anteriors and occlusal/buccal of lower molars [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: What distinguishes eating-disorder erosion from dietary erosion is the pattern: palatal surfaces of upper anteriors and occlusal/buccal of lower molars are the intrinsic acid targets [2], while dietary erosion classically affects labial surfaces of upper anteriors. The social history and the palatal predominance together point to the intrinsic source.
problems.treatment: These conditions warrant referral [2]. Dental management addresses the erosion — preventive measures, monitoring, and restorative intervention when dentine exposure causes symptoms or aesthetic concern. The priority is appropriate medical and psychological management of the eating disorder [1].
problems.prognosis: The underlying condition has a significant mortality rate [1]. Dental prognosis depends on the stage of erosion at presentation and whether the vomiting cycle can be interrupted. With medical management of the underlying disorder, erosion can be arrested and restored.

citations.quote: This is the development of weight reduction as an overvalued idea. Associated with weight ↓ of >25% of ideal body weight and obsessive food avoidance. Commonest in females, it is also associated with amenorrhea. Has a significant mortality rate; binge-eating followed by vomiting &/or laxative abuse can occur. Bingeing without weight loss is bulimia nervosa. Dental effects, …… Erosion, p. 252.

Acid from stomach due to gastro-oesophageal reflux, vomiting in relation to eating disorder (…… Anorexia nervosa/bulimia nervosa, p. 555), pregnancy, stress, or rumination. Such conditions warrant referral. Affects palatal surfaces of ULS and occlusal/buccal of lower molars.

problems.description: Progressive smooth palatal erosion on upper teeth, sometimes accompanied by dyspepsia, chronic sore throat, or cough. No obvious dietary acid source.
problems.etiology: Gastro-oesophageal reflux — regurgitation of gastric acid — is an intrinsic source of dental erosion. The same pattern as eating-disorder erosion is produced, but without vomiting behavior. GORD is a common cause of dyspepsia, sore throat, cough, and bad taste [1]. It may be entirely silent from the patient's perspective, with dental erosion as the presenting sign.
problems.presentation: What you'll typically hear: episodic heartburn, a sour taste, chronic sore throat, or morning hoarseness. Sometimes nothing dental-specific — the patient attends for a check-up and the erosion is found. Palatal erosion of upper incisors is the dental sign. The reason for the palatal pattern is that the refluxate pools on the palatal aspect of the upper teeth during or after reflux episodes.
problems.results: Smooth erosion predominantly on the palatal surfaces of upper anterior teeth, with possible involvement of occlusal surfaces of molars. Exposed dentine may trigger sensitivity. The pattern is intrinsic (palatal and occlusal) rather than extrinsic (labial) [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: GORD-related erosion shares the intrinsic acid pattern with eating-disorder erosion, but the history distinguishes them: no vomiting behavior, possible dyspepsia symptoms, and often a middle-aged or older patient rather than the young woman with weight concerns. Both warrant referral for the underlying condition [2].
problems.treatment: These conditions warrant referral [2]. Dental preventive measures: fluoride protection and avoid toothbrushing immediately after a reflux episode. Restorative management for sensitivity or aesthetics as required. Medical management of GORD reduces the acid load.
problems.prognosis: With medical management of GORD, dental erosion can be arrested. Existing tooth loss is irreversible; restorative management can replace lost tissue. Patients with ongoing reflux require monitoring for erosion progression.

citations.quote: Reflux oesophagitis is a common cause of dyspepsia, sore throat, cough, and bad taste.

Acid from stomach due to gastro-oesophageal reflux, vomiting in relation to eating disorder (…… Anorexia nervosa/bulimia nervosa, p. 555), pregnancy, stress, or rumination. Such conditions warrant referral. Affects palatal surfaces of ULS and occlusal/buccal of lower molars.

problems.description: Electric shock sensation or worsening ache along the lower jaw that increases during the day and decreases overnight. Patient wears a lower denture on a very resorbed ridge.
problems.etiology: Following alveolar resorption, the mental foramen migrates toward the ridge crest and the mental nerve may lie directly under the denture flange rather than protected within bone [1]. The denture compresses the nerve throughout the day — so the pain is worst after prolonged wear and lessens overnight when the denture is removed [1].
problems.presentation: What you'll hear: an electric-shock sensation or a background ache that builds through the day and settles overnight [1]. Leaving the lower denture out for several days reduces the pain [1]. The patient has usually worn the denture for years with gradual worsening as the ridge resorbs further.
problems.results: Clinical examination reveals a very resorbed lower ridge with the mental foramen at or near the ridge crest. Pressure over the foramen area reproduces the characteristic sensation. Radiograph shows the foramen close to or at the alveolar crest.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The pattern of daytime-loading pain that falls overnight is the defining feature [1]. The relief from leaving the denture out for several days is both diagnostic and therapeutic [1]. So the history alone often clinches the diagnosis before any examination is needed.
problems.treatment: Short-term: advise the patient to leave the denture out for several days to confirm the diagnosis and provide relief [1]. Definitive: relieve the denture flange over the mental foramen, or rebase the denture to redistribute load. If this fails, mental nerve repositioning creates a new foramen under the current position, or the nerve is laterally transposed into soft tissues in grossly atrophic mandibles [1]. Piezosurgery is useful here as using this tool to remove bone may be less likely to cause nerve damage [1].
problems.prognosis: Denture modification or relining often resolves the problem. Surgical repositioning is effective but reserved for cases where conservative management fails [1].

citations.quote: Mental nerve compression by a denture flange following alveolar resorption is a common problem, producing a sensation like an electric shock but with a background ache which ↑ during the day and ↓ overnight. Leaving the −/F out for several days ↓ the pain. The mental nerve is repositioned by creating a new foramen under its present position or laterally transposing the entire nerve into the soft tissues in grossly atrophic mandibles. Peizosurgery is useful here as using this tool to remove bone may be less likely to cause nerve damage.

problems.description: Delayed eruption and abnormal tooth structure in a child with skeletal deformity, leg bowing, or a history of nutritional deficiency.
problems.etiology: Rickets is failure of bone mineralisation in children (the adult equivalent is osteomalacia). The cause is deficiency, failure of synthesis, malabsorption, or impaired metabolism of vitamin D, and also hypophosphataemia or increased calcium requirement in pregnancy [1]. Among the systemic causes of delayed tooth eruption, rickets is listed alongside hereditary gingival fibromatosis, Down syndrome, Gardner syndrome, hypothyroidism, and cleidocranial dysostosis [2].
problems.presentation: The dental presentation is delayed eruption in the context of systemic features of rickets: skeletal deformity, leg bowing, growth retardation. Vitamin D-resistant rickets is additionally associated with dentinal abnormalities including dentinal dysplasia [3].
problems.results: Radiograph shows delayed development of tooth germs and delayed eruption. Enamel and dentine quality may be affected in vitamin D-resistant rickets. The systemic skeletal picture provides the diagnostic context.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The distinction from isolated delayed eruption is the systemic context: bone deformity or a known diagnosis of vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D-resistant rickets belongs to a small group of conditions causing dentinal abnormalities including dentinogenesis imperfecta and dentinal dysplasias [3].
problems.treatment: Manage the dental consequences — delayed eruption and any dentinal abnormalities. The underlying vitamin D deficiency or metabolic disorder requires medical management; refer to the appropriate team for the systemic condition.
problems.prognosis: Depends on the underlying cause and timing of medical treatment. With correction of vitamin D status, mineralisation normalises but existing dental structural defects are permanent.

problems.description: Jaw pain or an incidental bone lesion found on dental radiograph in a patient with chronic renal disease, on dialysis, or post-transplant.
problems.conditionName: Renal osteodystrophy (chronic kidney disease — oral and jaw manifestations)
problems.etiology: Chronic kidney disease produces progressive renal damage — commonly from glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, or polycystic disease — with protean systemic manifestations progressing to multisystem failure [1]. The jaw and dental consequences include bone lesions through renal osteodystrophy and secondary hyperparathyroidism [2]. Dialysis-dependent patients also carry increased infection risk (worsened by immunosuppression), increased bleeding tendency, and reduced drug excretion capacity [3][4].
problems.presentation: The patient is known to have chronic kidney disease or is on dialysis or post-transplant. Dental presentation may be jaw pain, jaw expansion, or loosening of teeth from the bony changes. Jaw lesions may alternatively be incidental radiographic findings. Generalised growth impairment may be present in children [2].
problems.results: Radiograph shows the jaw bone lesions associated with renal osteodystrophy and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Blood results in the medical history document the degree of renal failure.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The key practical rule: veins are sacrosanct in dialysis patients — never use their arteriovenous fistula [5]. That is the most immediately important dental team awareness. The jaw lesions are the oral signal of underlying metabolic bone disease, not a primary jaw pathology. Potential carriage of hepatitis B or HIV warrants cross-infection precautions [6].
problems.treatment: Medical management of the renal disease is primary. Dental treatment requires coordination with the renal team: timing around dialysis, caution with drug prescribing given reduced excretion capacity [4], awareness of increased bleeding tendency [3] and infection risk [3]. Never use the arteriovenous fistula [5].
problems.prognosis: The jaw bone lesions reflect the systemic metabolic state. Prognosis of the dental manifestations is tied to management of the underlying renal disease.

citations.quote: Basically the onset of uraemia after gradual, but progressive renal damage, commonly caused by glomerulonephritis (inflammation of the glomeruli following immune complex deposits), pyelonephritis (small scarred kidneys due to childhood infection, irradiation, or poisoning), or adult polycystic disease (congenital cysts within Bowman’s capsule). It has protean manifestations, starting with nocturia and anorexia, progressing through hypertension and anaemia to multisystem failure.
Bone lesions of the jaws (renal osteodystrophy, 2° hyperparathyroidism). Generalized growth impairment in children.

problems.description: Progressive jaw enlargement, spacing of teeth, Class III malocclusion, and macroglossia developing in an adult. A pituitary tumour may be known or suspected.
problems.etiology: Acromegaly is due to excess growth hormone production after closure of epiphyseal plates [1]. Before epiphyseal closure the same excess produces gigantism [2]. The oral and jaw changes are a direct result of growth hormone driving soft and hard tissue enlargement.
problems.presentation: What you'll see: enlargement of the tongue and lips, spacing of the teeth, and an increase in jaw size — particularly the mandible — resulting in a Class III malocclusion [1]. The patient may describe progressive jaw bite changes. Jaw pain is sometimes described [1].
problems.results: Clinical examination reveals prognathic mandible, macroglossia, macrocheilia, and tooth spacing [1]. Jaw pain may be present and can respond to treatment of the underlying pituitary tumour [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of macroglossia, tooth spacing, and mandibular prognathism in an adult with gradual onset points to excess growth hormone. Jaw pain that responds to treatment of the pituitary tumour is a useful pointer [1]. So this is a condition where the dental presentation may direct the diagnosis.
problems.treatment: The definitive treatment is trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy for the pituitary adenoma responsible [1]. Jaw pain can respond to treatment of the growth hormone-secreting tumour [1]. Dental and orthodontic management of the resultant malocclusion is secondary to addressing the endocrine source.
problems.prognosis: Tied to the outcome of pituitary tumour management. Jaw size changes and tooth spacing are irreversible once established.

problems.description: Teeth that are abnormally opalescent and wear rapidly. Patient has a history of multiple fractures from minor trauma, blue-tinged sclerae, or deafness.
problems.etiology: Osteogenesis imperfecta is an autosomal dominant type 1 collagen defect [1]. The systemic hallmarks are multiple fractures following slight trauma with rapid but distorted healing, blue sclerae, deafness, and dentinogenesis imperfecta [1]. The collagen defect affects the dentine matrix as well as bone collagen.
problems.presentation: Teeth appear opalescent (grey-brown or blue-brown) and wear rapidly because the dentine is structurally abnormal. The patient has a known or suspected systemic diagnosis of osteogenesis imperfecta. The combination of opalescent teeth and a fracture history in a young patient is the picture.
problems.results: Radiograph shows the classic dentinogenesis imperfecta pattern: bulbous crowns, constricted cervices, obliterated root canals, and shortened roots. Clinically, the enamel chips away, exposing the weak dentine, which wears rapidly.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason this matters in general practice: the first presentation may be the opalescent teeth, and the fracture history or blue sclerae may not yet have been formally diagnosed. The jaws are not particularly prone to fractures following extractions [1] — so routine dental extractions can be performed, but the systemic context requires awareness.
problems.treatment: Manage the dentinogenesis imperfecta: protective restorations, crowns, or overdentures to prevent further wear. Full mouth rehabilitation is often required in severe cases. Refer to a specialist paediatric dentist for children. No special extraction precautions are required specifically for the jaw fracture risk [1].
problems.prognosis: Dentinogenesis imperfecta in osteogenesis imperfecta follows the same course as isolated dentinogenesis imperfecta — teeth are susceptible to rapid wear but can be protected restoratively. The jaws are not particularly prone to fracture following extractions [1].

problems.description: Jaw infection that is extremely difficult to eradicate in a patient with unusually dense, sclerotic bone on radiograph. Frontal bossing and hypertelorism may be noted.
problems.etiology: Osteopetrosis involves an increase in bone density and brittleness, and a decrease in blood supply [1]. The reduced vascularity is the key: it makes infection in the jaw extremely difficult to eradicate [1]. Bone pain, fractures, and compression neuropathies may also occur [1]. Anaemia can complicate severe disease [1].
problems.presentation: The patient may present with a jaw infection that fails to resolve despite antibiotics and standard surgical drainage, in the context of a known or unknown diagnosis of osteopetrosis. Facial characteristics are frontal bossing and hypertelorism [1].
problems.results: Radiograph shows uniformly dense, marble-like bone with obliteration of the normal trabecular pattern. The mandible and maxilla appear sclerotic. In the context of osteomyelitis, the sclerotic bone limits drainage of pus and hinders healing.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason jaw infection is so hard to treat is the reduced blood supply [1]. Unlike normal osteomyelitis where surgical drainage usually resolves the infection, in osteopetrosis the avascular dense bone resists both infection-fighting and healing. Anaemia from marrow replacement adds to systemic vulnerability [1].
problems.treatment: Jaw infection in osteopetrosis requires specialist referral. Pre-operatively, discuss any planned extractions or surgical procedures with the patient's specialist team, given the elevated risk of osteomyelitis.
problems.prognosis: Jaw infections in osteopetrosis are prone to chronicity and are difficult to eradicate [1]. The prognosis depends on the severity of the underlying disease and degree of vascular compromise in the bone.

problems.description: Multiple unerupted permanent teeth retained beneath the gum, while primary teeth are still in place well into adulthood. Clavicle hypoplasia may be present.
problems.etiology: Cleidocranial dysostosis is an autosomal dominant defect of membranous bone formation [1][2]. The clavicles are affected (hypoplastic or absent), and the cranial fontanelles show delayed ossification [2]. What makes this most relevant in dentistry is the failure of tooth eruption with multiple supernumerary teeth and retention of the primary dentition [2]. The condition mainly affects membranous bone [2].
problems.presentation: The classic dental picture is: multiple unerupted permanent teeth, retention of primary dentition well beyond the normal exfoliation age, and multiple supernumerary teeth [2]. The skull is large and short with frontal and parietal bossing [2]. Shoulder mobility may be unusually wide because of clavicle hypoplasia.
problems.results: DPT shows a striking picture: multiple unerupted permanent teeth, often dozens of supernumerary teeth, and persistent primary teeth [2]. Inherent tooth abnormalities are common — dilaceration of roots, crown gemination, hypoplasia of secondary cementum [2]. A high-arched palate or clefting may be present [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining feature is the combination of multiple unerupted permanent teeth, supernumerary teeth, and persistent primary dentition in the context of a syndrome affecting membranous bone [2]. Skull and clavicle involvement separates this from simple hypodontia with retained primaries. Rickets, hypothyroidism, and Down syndrome are the other systemic causes of delayed eruption [3].
problems.treatment: Management is complex and multi-disciplinary: staged surgical exposure and extraction of supernumerary teeth to allow eruption or facilitate orthodontic traction of the permanent teeth. Specialist referral to a paediatric dentist and orthodontist is required early.
problems.prognosis: With staged surgical and orthodontic management, permanent teeth can often be brought into occlusion, but the treatment is prolonged. Unerupted teeth that cannot be brought into function require long-term monitoring for cyst formation.

citations.quote: An inherited defect of membranous bone formation, usually autosomal dominant. Skull and clavicles are affected. Multiple unerupted teeth with retention of 1° dentition is characteristic.

An autosomal dominant inherited condition consisting of hypoplasia or aplasia of the clavicles, delayed ossification of the cranial fontanelles, and a large, short skull. Associated features are shortness of stature, frontal and parietal bossing, failure to pneumatize the air sinuses, a high-arched palate &/or clefting, mid-face hypoplasia, and failure of tooth eruption with multiple supernumerary teeth. Many of the teeth present have inherent abnormalities such as dilaceration of roots or crown gemination. Hypoplasia of 2° cementum may occur. The condition mainly, though not exclusively, affects membranous bone.

problems.description: A syndrome of dense sclerotic bone on radiograph combined with micrognathia, exophthalmos, dwarfism, and short fingers. Presents rarely for dental or orthognathic assessment.
problems.etiology: Pycnodysostosis is characterised by micrognathia with hypoplasia of the mandibular angle, exophthalmos, dwarfism, short fingers, and osteopetrosis [1]. The osteopetrosis component carries the same implications as isolated osteopetrosis: increased bone density and brittleness with reduced blood supply.
problems.presentation: The patient presents rarely for orthognathic or orthodontic assessment [1]. The mandibular angle is hypoplastic, giving an abnormal jaw shape. The dense sclerotic bone pattern on radiograph will be noted. The clinician needs awareness of the osteopetrosis component before undertaking any dento-alveolar surgery.
problems.results: Radiograph shows dense sclerotic bone (osteopetrotic pattern). The mandibular angle is hypoplastic on clinical and radiographic examination.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason the osteopetrosis component is clinically important is the infection and healing risk for any jaw surgery or extractions. The combination of the facial dysmorphic features and the dense bone distinguishes pycnodysostosis from isolated osteopetrosis. So the rule here: be aware of the osteopetrosis before any surgical procedure [1].
problems.treatment: Be aware of the osteopetrosis [1]. Any dento-alveolar surgery carries an elevated risk of poor healing and infection. Discuss with the patient's specialist team before extractions or surgical procedures.
problems.prognosis: Rare presentations. The osteopetrosis component limits surgical options and increases infection risk, as in isolated osteopetrosis.

citations.quote: Micrognathia with hypoplasia of the mandibular angle, exophthalmos, dwarfism, short fingers, and osteopetrosis. Rarely present for orthognathic/orthodontic Rx. Be aware of the osteopetrosis.

problems.description: Congenitally missing multiple teeth in a child with sparse hair, absent or reduced sweating, and a characteristic saddle nose.
problems.etiology: Hypohydrotic ectodermal dysplasia combines hypodontia with lack of hair, lack of sweating, and a saddle nose [1]. The ectodermal defect affects structures derived from ectoderm: teeth (leading to hypodontia), hair follicles, and sweat glands. The result in the mouth is severe hypodontia, and where teeth are present they are often conical in shape.
problems.presentation: The child presents with severely reduced number of erupted teeth, or the primary dentition failed to erupt in normal numbers. The child may have sparse or absent hair, reduced sweating, and the characteristic saddle nose appearance [1]. Conical-shaped teeth where teeth are present is a diagnostic pointer.
problems.results: DPT shows severely reduced tooth germ development — marked hypodontia affecting both dentitions. Clinical examination confirms conical teeth where present. The facial appearance with saddle nose and the hair and sweating history complete the syndromic picture.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of hypodontia with ectodermal features — lack of hair and sweating and saddle nose — is the defining picture [1]. Isolated hypodontia does not have these systemic features. The medical importance of the reduced sweating should be flagged: these patients may be at risk of hyperthermia in hot conditions.
problems.treatment: Prosthetic rehabilitation is the dental goal: complete dentures or overdentures in children to restore function, aesthetics, and jaw development. Implants can be considered after skeletal maturity. Early specialist referral to a paediatric dentist and restorative specialist for long-term prosthetic planning.
problems.prognosis: The hypodontia is permanent. Prosthetic rehabilitation provides function and aesthetics but requires ongoing maintenance and upgrading through growth. With implant-retained restorations at maturity, long-term function is achievable.

problems.description: Dental erosion associated with a known or suspected gastrin-secreting tumour causing excessive acid production.
problems.conditionName: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (dental erosion from gastrin hypersecretion)
problems.etiology: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumour that drives excessive acid production, causing duodenal ulcers and diarrhoea [1]. The intrinsic acid erosion pattern on the teeth is the same as for GORD — palatal surfaces of upper anteriors and occlusal surfaces — but the underlying cause is a gastrinoma.
problems.presentation: The patient typically carries a known medical diagnosis of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome or has recalcitrant peptic ulcer disease under investigation. The dental finding is erosion of the intrinsic acid pattern. The clinical context distinguishes this from dietary erosion.
problems.results: Smooth erosion on palatal and occlusal surfaces following the intrinsic acid pattern. The medical history and gastrin levels establish the diagnosis. The dental picture alone cannot distinguish Zollinger–Ellison erosion from GORD or eating-disorder erosion — the systemic context is the differentiator.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason for noting this condition: recalcitrant erosion in a patient with confirmed or suspected peptic disease warrants medical investigation. Zollinger–Ellison syndrome and GORD both produce the intrinsic acid erosion pattern; the distinction is the underlying gastrin-secreting tumour [1].
problems.treatment: Medical management of the gastrinoma is primary. Dental management as for intrinsic erosion: preventive measures, fluoride protection, avoid toothbrushing immediately after acid exposure, and restorative management of tooth loss as required.
problems.prognosis: Dental erosion from Zollinger–Ellison syndrome is reversible by controlling the acid source; irreversible once tooth structure is lost. Medical management of the gastrinoma reduces the dental risk.

problems.description: A restoration that was placed to match adjacent teeth now looks visibly different — discoloured, opaque, or mismatched — causing patient concern.
problems.etiology: Failed restoration aesthetics may arise from underlying discolouration (stained dentine beneath or corrosion products from underlying metal) or from surface staining of the restoration itself [1]. The cause determines the management: surface staining can sometimes be polished; underlying dentine discolouration or corroded metal requires replacement.
problems.presentation: The patient reports dissatisfaction with the appearance of a tooth — a filling, crown, or veneer that no longer matches. The restoration may have been fine initially and discoloured over time, or may never have matched well. The question is whether the patient is actually concerned: it is worth checking before replacing [1].
problems.results: Visual examination identifies the nature of the discolouration — surface stain (removable by polishing), intrinsic discolouration (stained dentine visible through the restoration), or metal corrosion products at the margin. Translucency and shade of the restoration are assessed against adjacent teeth.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The interesting bit in practice: the clinician’s assessment of a failed aesthetic may not match the patient’s concern. Patients may not be concerned, so it is worth checking before replacing [1]. Replacing a restoration purely for aesthetics that doesn’t bother the patient is unnecessary treatment.
problems.treatment: Check whether the patient is actually concerned before committing to replacement [1]. If surface staining: attempt polish. If underlying discolouration or corrosion products: assess whether replacement is indicated and what material will best achieve the desired result.
problems.prognosis: Aesthetic restorations have a finite lifespan before colour change requires attention. Surface staining can be managed conservatively. Underlying causes such as stained dentine or corroded metal require restoration replacement.

citations.quote: This may be due to underlying discoloration from stained dentine or corrosion products or superficial from surface staining. Patients may not be concerned so it is worth checking before replacing.

problems.description: A visible gap or step at the edge of a restoration — 'ditching' around an amalgam or a chipped margin on a composite — with or without sensitivity.
problems.etiology: Failed marginal integrity can result from creep and corrosion causing ditching of amalgam restorations, shrinkage of composites or GIC at the margin, or marginal chipping [1]. The clinical significance depends on plaque control: if the patient can keep the margin plaque-free and there is no recurrent caries, replacement may not be necessary [2].
problems.presentation: The patient may report sensitivity, food packing, or may have noticed the step. Often found incidentally on routine examination. The margin is visible as a gap, step, or roughness at the restoration boundary.
problems.results: Visual and tactile examination identifies marginal ditching, gap, or chip. Bitewing radiograph is the investigation for secondary caries. The threshold for intervention is evidence of dentine involvement with progression or cavitation — not the mere presence of a marginal defect [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The rule here: a marginal defect without secondary caries and with a plaque-free patient does not automatically require replacement [2]. Secondary caries is difficult to diagnose, and careful observation rather than intervention is now advocated [2]. Intervention is indicated only when the lesion is in dentine with evidence of progression and/or cavitation [2].
problems.treatment: If the patient can keep the margin plaque-free and there is no recurrent caries: careful observation rather than replacement [2]. If secondary caries is present in dentine with progression or cavitation: replace the restoration [2]. To prevent secondary caries: educate the patient to reduce their caries rate and ensure an excellent restorative technique for any replacement [2].
problems.prognosis: Marginal defects alone do not inevitably progress to caries — plaque control is the determining factor [2]. Where secondary caries does develop, early identification on bitewing radiograph and timely replacement prevents further breakdown.

citations.quote: This can be due to creep/corrosion and ditching of amalgams or shrinkage of composites/GIC or marginal chipping.

If the patient can keep the margin plaque free and there is no recurrent caries then it may not be necessary to replace the restoration. If not, 2° or recurrent caries may be a risk. 2° caries is difficult to diagnose, but careful observation (clinically and radiographically) rather than intervention, is now advocated. Intervention is only indicated when the lesion is in dentine, and there is evidence of progression &/or cavitation is present. To prevent 2° caries it is important not only to educate the patient to reduce their caries rate but also to use an excellent restorative technique to ensure good long term-restorations.

problems.description: A large part of a restoration fractures off, leaving the tooth partly exposed. Often happens on an occlusal surface under heavy load.
problems.etiology: Bulk fracture of a restoration can be due to heavy occlusal loading, poor cavity design, or poor bonding [1]. The failure is not random — it reflects either a material placed in an under-supported cavity, a bonding failure at the interface, or simply a load greater than the restoration was designed to carry.
problems.presentation: The patient notices a sudden loss of part of the restoration — often felt as a sharp edge on the tongue. There may be sensitivity from exposed dentine, or no symptoms if the fracture left remaining material over the dentine. The tooth may be visually obvious on examination.
problems.results: Visual examination shows the fractured restoration with exposed dentine or a portion of remaining material. Percussion is not tender unless secondary pulpal or periapical involvement has developed. Sensibility testing positive if the pulp is vital.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The distinction from marginal ditching: here the bulk of the restoration is lost, not just the margin. The reason matters for planning replacement: if the fracture was due to heavy loading or poor cavity design, the replacement must address those factors — cusp coverage, improved bonding, or a material better matched to the occlusal load [1].
problems.treatment: Replace the restoration. Assess the reason for failure: heavy occlusal loading (consider cuspal coverage or indirect restoration), poor cavity design (redesign with adequate cuspal support), or poor bonding (address bonding protocol) [1].
problems.prognosis: Bulk fracture restorations can be replaced, but without addressing the underlying cause the replacement will fail again. Heavy occlusal loading may ultimately require an indirect restoration or crown to distribute the load across remaining tooth structure.
